<span class="atom-split" data-atom="the_narrative_of_a_gordon_pym_raven_edition" data-title="The Narrative of A. Gordon Pym (Raven Edition)" data-chapter="" data-kind="intro"></span>


INTRODUCTORY NOTE



Upon my return to the United States a few months ago, after the

extraordinary series of adventure in the South Seas and

elsewhere, of which an account is given in the following pages,

accident threw me into the society of several gentlemen in

Richmond, Va., who felt deep interest in all matters relating to

the regions I had visited, and who were constantly urging it upon

me, as a duty, to give my narrative to the public. I had several

reasons, however, for declining to do so, some of which were of a

[[concepts/nature|nature]] altogether private, and concern no person but myself;

others not so much so. One consideration which deterred me was

that, having kept no journal during a greater portion of the [[motifs/time|time]]

in which I was absent, I feared I should not be able to write,

from mere [[motifs/memory|memory]], a statement so minute and connected as to have

the _appearance_of that [[concepts/truth|truth]] it would really possess, barring

only the natural and unavoidable exaggeration to which all of us

are prone when detailing events which have had powerful influence

in exciting the imaginative faculties. Another reason was, that

the incidents to be narrated were of a [[concepts/nature|nature]] so positively

marvellous that, unsupported as my assertions must necessarily be

(except by the evidence of a single individual, and he a

half-breed Indian), I could only [[concepts/hope|hope]] for belief among my family,

and those of my friends who have had reason, through life, to put

[[concepts/faith|faith]] in my veracity—the probability being that the public at

large would regard what I should put forth as merely an impudent

and ingenious fiction. A distrust in my own abilities as a writer

was, nevertheless, one of the principal causes which prevented me

from complying with the suggestions of my advisers.



Among those gentlemen in Virginia who expressed the greatest

interest in my statement, more particularly in regard to that

portion of it which related to the Antarctic Ocean, was Mr. Poe,

lately editor of the “Southern Literary Messenger,” a monthly

magazine, published by Mr. Thomas W. White, in the [[motifs/city|city]] of

Richmond. He strongly advised me, among others, to prepare at

once a full account of what I had seen and undergone, and trust

to the shrewdness and common-sense of the public—insisting, with

great plausibility, that however roughly, as regards mere

authorship, my book should be got up, its very uncouthness, if

there were any, would give it all the better chance of being

received as [[concepts/truth|truth]].



Notwithstanding this representation, I did not make up my mind to

do as he suggested. He afterward proposed (finding that I would

not stir in the matter) that I should allow him to draw up, in

his own words, a narrative of the earlier portion of my

adventures, from facts afforded by myself, publishing it in the

“Southern Messenger” _under the garb of fiction. _To this,

perceiving no objection, I consented, stipulating only that my

real name should be retained. Two numbers of the pretended

fiction appeared, consequently, in the “Messenger” for January

and February (1837), and, in order that it might certainly be

regarded as fiction, the name of Mr. Poe was affixed to the

articles in the table of contents of the magazine.



The manner in which this ruse was received has induced me at

length to undertake a regular compilation and publication of the

adventures in question; for I found that, in spite of the air of

[[forms/fable|fable]] which had been so ingeniously thrown around that portion of

my statement which appeared in the “Messenger” (without altering

or distorting a single fact), the public were still not at all

disposed to receive it as [[forms/fable|fable]], and several letters were sent to

Mr. P.’s address, distinctly expressing a conviction to the

contrary. I thence concluded that the facts of my narrative would

prove of such a [[concepts/nature|nature]] as to carry with them sufficient evidence

of their own authenticity, and that I had consequently little to

[[concepts/fear|fear]] on the score of popular [[Incredulity|incredulity]].



This _exposé_being made, it will be seen at once how much of what

follows I claim to be my own writing; and it will also be

understood that no fact is misrepresented in the first few pages

which were written by Mr. Poe. Even to those readers who have not

seen the “Messenger,” it will be unnecessary to point out where

his portion ends and my own commences; the difference in point of

style will be readily perceived.



A. G. PYM.

CHAPTER 1





My name is [[characters/arthur|Arthur]] Gordon Pym. My father was a respectable trader

in sea-stores at Nantucket, where I was born. My maternal

grandfather was an attorney in good practice. He was fortunate in

every thing, and had speculated very successfully in stocks of

the Edgarton New Bank, as it was formerly called. By these and

other means he had managed to lay by a tolerable sum of money. He

was more attached to myself, I believe, than to any other person

in the world, and I expected to inherit the most of his property

at his [[motifs/death|death]]. He sent me, at six years of age, to the school of

old Mr. Ricketts, a gentleman with only one arm and of eccentric

manners—he is [[motifs/well|well]] known to almost every person who has visited

New Bedford. I stayed at his school until I was sixteen, when I

left him for Mr. E. Ronald’s academy on the [[motifs/hill|hill]]. Here I became

intimate with the son of Mr. Barnard, a sea-captain, who

generally sailed in the employ of Lloyd and Vredenburgh—Mr.

Barnard is also very [[motifs/well|well]] known in New Bedford, and has many

relations, I am certain, in Edgarton. His son was named Augustus,

and he was nearly two years older than myself. He had been on a

whaling voyage with his father in the John Donaldson, and was

always talking to me of his adventures in the South Pacific

Ocean. I used frequently to go [[motifs/home|home]] with him, and remain all day,

and sometimes all [[motifs/night|night]]. We occupied the same bed, and he would

be sure to keep me awake until almost light, telling me stories

of the natives of the Island of Tinian, and other places he had

visited in his travels. At last I could not help being interested

in what he said, and by degrees I felt the greatest [[motifs/desire|desire]] to go

to sea. I owned a sailboat called the [[characters/ariel|Ariel]], and worth about

seventy-five dollars. She had a half-deck or cuddy, and was

rigged sloop-fashion—I forget her tonnage, but she would hold ten

persons without much crowding. In this boat we were in the habit

of going on some of the maddest freaks in the world; and, when I

now think of them, it appears to me a thousand wonders that I am

alive to-day.



I will relate one of these adventures by way of introduction to a

longer and more momentous narrative. One [[motifs/night|night]] there was a party

at Mr. Barnard’s, and both Augustus and myself were not a little

intoxicated toward the close of it. As usual, in such cases, I

took part of his bed in preference to going [[motifs/home|home]]. He went to

[[motifs/sleep|sleep]], as I thought, very quietly (it being near one when the

party broke up), and without saying a word on his favorite topic.

It might have been half an hour from the [[motifs/time|time]] of our getting in

bed, and I was just about falling into a doze, when he suddenly

started up, and swore with a terrible oath that he would not go

to [[motifs/sleep|sleep]] for any [[characters/arthur|Arthur]] Pym in Christendom, when there was so

glorious a breeze from the southwest. I never was so astonished

in my life, not knowing what he intended, and thinking that the

wines and liquors he had drunk had set him entirely beside

himself. He proceeded to talk very coolly, however, saying he

knew that I supposed him intoxicated, but that he was never more

sober in his life. He was only tired, he added, of lying in bed

on such a fine [[motifs/night|night]] like a dog, and was determined to get up and

dress, and go out on a frolic with the boat. I can hardly tell

what possessed me, but the words were no sooner out of his mouth

than I felt a thrill of the greatest excitement and pleasure, and

thought his mad idea one of the most delightful and most

reasonable things in the world. It was blowing almost a gale, and

the weather was very cold—it being late in October. I sprang out

of bed, nevertheless, in a kind of ecstasy, and told him I was

quite as brave as himself, and quite as tired as he was of lying

in bed like a dog, and quite as ready for any fun or frolic as

any Augustus Barnard in Nantucket.



We lost no [[motifs/time|time]] in getting on our clothes and hurrying down to

the boat. She was lying at the old decayed wharf by the

lumber-yard of Pankey & Co., and almost thumping her side out

against the rough logs. Augustus got into her and bailed her, for

she was nearly half full of [[motifs/water|water]]. This being done, we hoisted

jib and mainsail, kept full, and started boldly out to sea.



The [[motifs/wind|wind]], as I before said, blew freshly from the southwest. The

[[motifs/night|night]] was very clear and cold. Augustus had taken the helm, and I

stationed myself by the mast, on the deck of the cuddy. We flew

along at a great rate—neither of us having said a word since

casting loose from the wharf. I now asked my companion what

course he intended to steer, and what [[motifs/time|time]] he thought it probable

we should get back. He whistled for a few minutes, and then said

crustily: “_I_ am going to sea—_you_ may go [[motifs/home|home]] if you think

proper.” Turning my eyes upon him, I perceived at once that, in

spite of his assumed _nonchalance_, he was greatly agitated. I

could see him distinctly by the light of the [[motifs/moon|moon]]—his face was

paler than any marble, and his hand shook so excessively that he

could scarcely retain hold of the tiller. I found that something

had gone wrong, and became seriously alarmed. At this period I

knew little about the management of a boat, and was now depending

entirely upon the nautical skill of my friend. The [[motifs/wind|wind]], too, had

Il mio nome è [[characters/arthur|Arthur]] Gordon Pym. Mio padre era un rispettabile commerciante.

“Nei negozi di souvenir di Nantucket, dove sono nato… Quelli legati alla mia famiglia materna.”

Il nonno era un avvocato molto impegnato nel suo lavoro. Ebbe la fortuna di…

Tutto… e aveva fatto delle speculazioni molto proficue sulle azioni.

Il nuovo edificio della banca di Edgarton, come veniva chiamato in passato…

Con altri mezzi, era riuscito ad accumulare una somma di denaro considerevole. Lui…

Credo di essere stato più legato a me stesso che a qualsiasi altra persona.

Nel mondo intero, e mi aspettavo di ereditare la maggior parte dei suoi beni.

Al momento della sua [[motifs/death|morte]], mi mandò, all’età di sei anni, alla scuola.

New Bedford. Sono rimasto nella sua scuola fino ai sedici anni…

Intimo del figlio di Mr. Barnard, un capitano di mare…

Di solito navigava al servizio di Lloyd e Vredenburgh, il signor.

Barnard è anche molto conosciuto a New Bedford e ha molti.

Relazioni… Ne sono certo, ad Edgarton. Suo figlio si chiamava Augustus.

E lui era quasi due anni più grande di me… Aveva già vissuto…

Viaggio di caccia alle balene con suo padre a bordo del John Donaldson, e…

Sempre mi parla delle sue avventure nel Sud del Pacifico

Oceano. In passato andavo spesso a [[motifs/home|casa]] con lui e rimanevo lì tutto il giorno.

E a volte, per tutta la [[motifs/night|notte]], condividevamo lo stesso letto; lui.

“Assicurati di tenermi sveglio fino quasi all’alba, raccontandomi storie…”

Titolo:  
Dei nativi dell’isola di Tinian e di altri luoghi che aveva visitato

Visitate durante i suoi viaggi… Alla fine non potei fare a meno di interessarmene.

Nelle sue parole, gradualmente provai il più grande desiderio di andare.

In mare. Possedevo un veliero chiamato [[characters/ariel|Ariel]], che valeva circa.

Settantacinque dollari… Aveva una piccola cabina, o meglio, un angolo ristretto dove riposare…

Una goletta allestita in quel modo… Non ricordo esattamente la sua stazza, ma poteva contenere dieci persone.

Persone senza troppa affollamento… In questa barca, avevamo l’abitudine di…

Titolo:  
Tra le più folli e stravaganti avventure del mondo… e quando io…

Ora che ci penso, mi sembrano mille meraviglie il fatto che io esista…

Vivo ancora oggi.



Titolo:  
Racconterò uno di questi avventuri come introduzione…

Un racconto più lungo e significativo. Una [[motifs/night|notte]], ci fu una festa.

Alla casa del signor Barnard… e sia Augustus che io eravamo piuttosto sorpresi

“Intossicato verso la fine… Come al solito, in questi casi…”

Preferì occupare metà del suo letto piuttosto che andare a [[motifs/home|casa]]. Andò.

Il [[motifs/sleep|sonno]], come pensavo, molto silenziosamente, poiché era quasi l’una di notte.

La festa finì, e senza pronunciare una parola sul suo argomento preferito.

Doveva essere passata mezz'ora dal momento in cui siamo entrati.

Quando stavo per addormentarmi…

“Si alzò in piedi e giurò con un’orribile imprecazione che non se ne sarebbe andato.”

Per qualsiasi [[characters/arthur|Arthur]] Pym in tutto il Cristianesimo, sarebbe stato impossibile dormire in quelle circostanze.

Una brezza meravigliosa proveniente dal sud-ovest… Non ero mai stato così sorpreso.

“Nella mia vita, senza sapere cosa intendesse lui, e pensando che…”

I vini e i liquori che aveva bevuto lo avevano completamente ubriacato.

Si parlò da solo. Tuttavia, continuò a parlare in modo molto calmo, dicendo…

Sapevo che doveva essere ubriaco, ma in realtà non lo era mai stato.

“Sobrio nella sua vita… Era solo stanco, aggiunse, di stare a letto.”

In una così bella [[motifs/night|notte]], si comportava come un cane, ed era deciso a alzarsi e.

Vestiti e vai a divertirti in barca… A malapena riesco a capire cosa intendi dire.

Che cosa mi aveva posseduto… Ma quelle parole non erano ancora finite di uscire dalla sua bocca

Una scossa di grande emozione e piacere…

Riteneva la sua idea folle una delle più deliziose e delle più…

Cose ragionevoli nel mondo… Soffiava quasi un uragano…

Il tempo era molto freddo; eravamo a fine ottobre. Sono uscito di scatto…

“Di letto, tuttavia, in una sorta di estasi, e gli dissi che ero…”

Altrettanto coraggiosa di lui, e altrettanto stanca delle menzogne che doveva dire…

A letto come un cane… e altrettanto pronto per qualsiasi gioco o scherzo.

Qualsiasi Augustus Barnard a Nantucket.



Non abbiamo perso nemmeno un minuto a vestirci e ci siamo affrettati a scendere.

Il barco… Giaceva presso il vecchio molo in rovina.

Il cortile di legname di Pankey & Co., e quasi la schiacciava contro il muro

“Contro i tronchi ruvidi… Augustus si infilò dentro di lei e la salvò.”

Era quasi piena a metà di [[motifs/water|acqua]]. Una volta fatto questo, abbiamo issato.

Vela di trinchetto e vela maestra, tese al massimo, e partì coraggiosamente verso il mare.



Il [[motifs/wind|vento]], come ho detto prima, soffiava fresco dal sud-ovest.

La [[motifs/night|notte]] era molto chiara e fredda. Augustus aveva preso il timone, e io.

Mi posizionai vicino al albero maestro, sul ponte della barca… Volammo.

“Avanzando a grande velocità… nessuno di noi ha detto una parola da allora.”

“Liberandomi dal molo… Ora chiesi al mio compagno cosa…”

Il percorso che intendeva seguire, e a quale [[motifs/time|ora]] pensava fosse probabile intraprenderlo.

“Dovremmo tornare indietro.” Soffiò nel fischio per alcuni minuti, poi disse…

Con tono brusco: “Io andrò in mare. Tu puoi tornare a [[motifs/home|casa]] se vuoi.”

“Proprio così.” Girando lo sguardo verso di lui, notai immediatamente che…

Nonostante la sua apparente indifferenza, era in realtà molto agitato.

Riuscivo a vederlo chiaramente alla luce della [[motifs/moon|luna]]; il suo viso era.

Più pallido di qualsiasi marmo, e la sua mano tremava così tanto che…

A malapena riuscivo a tenere il timone… Scoprii che qualcosa…

Qualcosa era andato storto, e in quel momento provai una seria preoccupazione. In quel periodo…

Conosceva poco riguardo alla gestione di una barca, e ora dipendeva da altri per farlo.

Interamente dipendeva dall'abilità navale di mio amico. Anche il [[motifs/wind|vento]] era favorevole.



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_01--part_02" data-title="The Narrative of A. Gordon Pym (Raven Edition) — Chapter 1 (part 2)" data-chapter="Chapter 01" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="motif/blood,motif/death,motif/home,motif/night,motif/rose,motif/ship,motif/silence,motif/storm,motif/time,motif/water,motif/well,motif/wind,concept/body,concept/despair,concept/doubt,concept/freedom,concept/madness,concept/truth,setting/ship,character/bottom"></span>


suddenly increased, as we were fast getting out of the lee of the

land—still I was ashamed to betray any trepidation, and for

almost half an hour maintained a resolute [[motifs/silence|silence]]. I could stand

it no longer, however, and spoke to Augustus about the propriety

of turning back. As before, it was nearly a minute before he made

answer, or took any notice of my suggestion. “By-and-by,” said he

at length—“[[motifs/time|time]] enough—[[motifs/home|home]] by-and-by.” I had expected a similar

reply, but there was something in the tone of these words which

filled me with an indescribable feeling of dread. I again looked

at the speaker attentively. His lips were perfectly livid, and

his knees shook so violently together that he seemed scarcely

able to stand. “For God’s sake, Augustus,” I screamed, now

heartily frightened, “what ails you?—what is the matter?—what

_are_ you going to do?” “Matter!” he stammered, in the greatest

apparent surprise, letting go the tiller at the same moment, and

falling forward into the [[characters/bottom|bottom]] of the boat—“matter—why, nothing

is the—matter—going [[motifs/home|home]]—d—d—don’t you see?” The whole [[concepts/truth|truth]] now

flashed upon me. I flew to him and raised him up. He was

drunk—beastly drunk—he could no longer either stand, speak, or

see. His eyes were perfectly glazed; and as I let him go in the

extremity of my [[concepts/despair|despair]], he rolled like a mere log into the

bilge-[[motifs/water|water]], from which I had lifted him. It was evident that,

during the evening, he had drunk far more than I suspected, and

that his conduct in bed had been the result of a

highly-concentrated state of intoxication—a state which, like

[[concepts/madness|madness]], frequently enables the victim to imitate the outward

demeanour of one in perfect possession of his senses. The

coolness of the [[motifs/night|night]] air, however, had had its usual effect—the

mental energy began to yield before its influence—and the

confused perception which he no [[concepts/doubt|doubt]] then had of his perilous

situation had assisted in hastening the catastrophe. He was now

thoroughly insensible, and there was no probability that he would

be otherwise for many hours.



It is hardly possible to conceive the extremity of my terror. The

fumes of the wine lately taken had evaporated, leaving me doubly

timid and irresolute. I knew that I was altogether incapable of

managing the boat, and that a fierce [[motifs/wind|wind]] and strong ebb tide

were hurrying us to destruction. A [[motifs/storm|storm]] was evidently gathering

behind us; we had neither compass nor provisions; and it was

clear that, if we held our present course, we should be out of

sight of land before daybreak. These thoughts, with a crowd of

others equally fearful, flashed through my mind with a

bewildering rapidity, and for some moments paralyzed me beyond

the possibility of making any exertion. The boat was going

through the [[motifs/water|water]] at a terrible rate—full before the [[motifs/wind|wind]]—no reef

in either jib or mainsail—running her bows completely under the

foam. It was a thousand wonders she did not broach to—Augustus

having let go the tiller, as I said before, and I being too much

agitated to think of taking it myself. By good luck, however, she

kept steady, and gradually I recovered some degree of presence of

mind. Still the [[motifs/wind|wind]] was increasing fearfully, and whenever we

[[motifs/rose|rose]] from a plunge forward, the sea behind fell combing over our

counter, and deluged us with [[motifs/water|water]]. I was so utterly benumbed,

too, in every limb, as to be nearly unconscious of sensation. At

length I summoned up the resolution of [[concepts/despair|despair]], and rushing to

the mainsail let it go by the run. As might have been expected,

it flew over the bows, and, getting drenched with [[motifs/water|water]], carried

away the mast short off by the board. This latter accident [[Alone|alone]]

saved me from instant destruction. Under the jib only, I now

boomed along before the [[motifs/wind|wind]], shipping heavy seas occasionally

over the counter, but relieved from the terror of immediate

[[motifs/death|death]]. I took the helm, and breathed with greater [[concepts/freedom|freedom]] as I

found that there yet remained to us a chance of ultimate escape.

Augustus still lay senseless in the [[characters/bottom|bottom]] of the boat; and as

there was imminent danger of his drowning (the [[motifs/water|water]] being nearly

a foot deep just where he fell), I contrived to raise him

partially up, and keep him in a sitting position, by passing a

rope round his waist, and lashing it to a ringbolt in the deck of

the cuddy. Having thus arranged every thing as [[motifs/well|well]] as I could in

my chilled and agitated condition, I recommended myself to God,

and made up my mind to bear whatever might happen with all the

fortitude in my power.



Hardly had I come to this resolution, when, suddenly, a loud and

long scream or yell, as if from the throats of a thousand demons,

seemed to pervade the whole atmosphere around and above the boat.

Never while I live shall I forget the intense agony of terror I

experienced at that moment. My hair stood erect on my head—I felt

the [[motifs/blood|blood]] congealing in my veins—my heart ceased utterly to beat,

and without having once raised my eyes to learn the source of my

alarm, I tumbled headlong and insensible upon the [[concepts/body|body]] of my

fallen companion.



I found myself, upon reviving, in the cabin of a large

whaling-[[motifs/ship|ship]] (the Penguin) bound to Nantucket. Several persons

Il volume aumentò improvvisamente, mentre ci allontanavamo rapidamente dall’area protetta…

Titolo:  
Terra… Eppure mi vergognavo di mostrare anche la minima esitazione…

Per quasi mezz’ora mantenne un risoluto [[motifs/silence|silenzio]]; riuscivo a sopportarlo.

Ora non più, tuttavia… e parlò con Augusto della opportunità di farlo.

Titolo:  
Di tornare indietro. Come prima, ci volle quasi un minuto prima che lui decidesse di farlo.

“Nessuno ha risposto né prestato attenzione alla mia proposta. ‘Col tempo…’, disse lui.”

Finalmente, “Abbastanza tempo. Tra poco saremo a casa.” Mi aspettavo qualcosa del genere.

Risposta… ma c’era qualcosa nel tono di quelle parole che…

Mi colmò di un senso di terrore indescrivibile… Guardai di nuovo.

Ascoltava il parlante con attenzione; le sue labbra erano pallide come la morte…

Le sue ginocchia tremavano così violentemente che sembrava quasi…

“Per l’amor di Dio, Augustus…”, gridai.

“Spaventata a morte… Che cosa ti è successo? Che c’è?”

“Cosa farai?” “Importante!” balbettò, con grande…

Con un’apparente sorpresa, lasciò andare il timone nello stesso istante…

Cadendo in avanti verso il fondo della barca, “Niente, perché, davvero niente.”

“La questione non sta forse per risolversi, non lo vedi? Ora tutta la [[concepts/truth|verità]] è finalmente chiara.”

Mi balenò in mente… Corsi da lui e lo sollevai. Lui era…

Ubriaco fradicio… non riusciva più nemmeno a stare in piedi, né a parlare, né a fare nulla.

“Vedi… I suoi occhi erano completamente vitidi; e mentre lo lasciavo entrare…”

Nel momento più estremo della mia [[concepts/despair|-disperazione]], rotolò via come un semplice tronco.

Acqua di sentina, dall’acqua di sentina che lo avevo tirato fuori. Era evidente che.

Durante la serata, aveva bevuto molto di più di quanto io immaginassi…

Il suo comportamento a letto era il risultato di…

Lo stato di ebbrezza estrema: uno stato che, proprio come…

La [[concepts/madness|pazzia]], spesso permette alla vittima di imitare il comportamento esteriore dell’aggressore.

Comportamento di chi possiede pienamente i propri sensi.

La freschezza dell’aria notturna, tuttavia, aveva avuto il solito effetto.

Energia mentale iniziò ad indebolirsi sotto la sua influenza… e poi…

Una percezione confusa, di cui all’epoca non aveva alcun [[concepts/doubt|dubbio]], riguardo al pericolo che lo minacciava.

La situazione aveva contribuito ad accelerare la catastrofe. Ora…

Del tutto insensibile… e non c’era alcuna possibilità che cambiasse.

Altrimenti, sarebbe durato molte ore.



È quasi impossibile immaginare l’intensità del mio terrore.

“Il fumo del vino che avevo bevuto poco prima si era dissipato, lasciandomi in uno stato particolare…”

Timido e indeciso… Sapevo di essere completamente incapace di…

Guidare la barca, e in più un violento [[motifs/wind|vento]] e una forte marea montante.

Ci spingevano verso la distruzione. Chiaramente si stava formando una [[motifs/storm|tempesta]].

Dietro di noi; non avevamo né bussola né provviste; e…

“Chiaramente, se continueremo per la strada attuale, finiremo nei guai.”

“La vista della terra prima dell’alba… Questi pensieri, insieme a tanti altri…”

“Altri altrettanto spaventati…”, mi passò per la mente.

Una velocità sconcertante… che per alcuni momenti mi ha lasciato completamente paralizzato

La possibilità di compiere qualsiasi sforzo… La barca proseguiva la sua corsa.

Attraverso l’[[motifs/water|acqua]] a una velocità terribile, riempito prima ancora che arrivasse il [[motifs/wind|vento]], nessun scoglio.

In vela di trinchetto o maestra… con la prua completamente immersa sotto l’acqua

“Spuma… Mille meraviglie che non menzionò mai… Augusto”

Abbandonando il timone, come ho detto prima… e essendo io stesso troppo…

Agitata all’idea di doverlo fare da sola… Ma per fortuna, lei…

Mantenuto costante… e gradualmente ho riacquistato una certa presenza di mente.

La mente. Comunque, il [[motifs/wind|vento]] aumentava di intensità in modo spaventoso, e ogni volta che.

Le [[motifs/rose|rose]], raccolte durante un tuffo in avanti, ci circondarono mentre il mare alle nostre spalle si ritirava.

Il contatore, e ci inondò di [[motifs/water|acqua]]. Ero completamente intorpidito.

In ogni parte del corpo, al punto di essere quasi privi di sensazioni…

Con grande determinazione, riuscii a superare lo [[concepts/despair|dispero]] e mi affrettai a.

La vela maestra si lasciò portare dal vento… Come ci si poteva aspettare.

Volò sopra le vele e, bagnandosi completamente nell’[[motifs/water|acqua]], continuò il suo percorso.

Lontano dal palo, tagliato proprio vicino alla tavola. Quest’ultimo incidente, [[Alone|solo]].

Mi ha salvato dalla distruzione immediata… Ora, soltanto sotto la gabbia di poppa…

Si diffondeva lungo il vento, attraversando di tanto in tanto mari agitati.

Fuori rete, ma liberato dal terrore dell’immediato

La [[motifs/death|morte]]. Presi il timone e respirai con maggiore [[concepts/freedom|libertà]] mentre.

Scoprimmo che ancora ci restava una possibilità di fuga definitiva.

Augusto giaceva ancora privo di sensi nella parte inferiore della barca; e mentre.

C’era un pericolo imminente che annegasse, poiché l’[[motifs/water|acqua]] era quasi.

(#Un piede di fango proprio dove è caduto… Riuscii comunque a sollevarlo)

Parzialmente sollevato e mantenuto in posizione seduta, passandogli…

"#Una corda intorno alla vita, legata a un anello di ferro sul ponte..."

Il rifugio accogliente. Dopo aver sistemato tutto nel modo migliore possibile, secondo le mie capacità.

Nella mia condizione di freddo e agitazione, mi affidai a Dio.

E decisi di affrontare qualsiasi cosa potesse accadere con coraggio.

La forza d'animo è qualcosa che mi appartiene.



Appena presi questa decisione, improvvisamente…

Un urlo lungo e straziante, come se provenisse dalle gole di mille demoni…

Sembrava permeare l’intera atmosfera intorno e sopra la barca.

Mai, finché vivrò, dimenticherò l’intensa angoscia e il terrore che ho provato

In quel momento provai una sensazione intensa… I miei capelli si rizzarono tutti in piedi; mi sentii…

Il [[motifs/blood|sangue]] si stava coagulando nelle mie vene; il mio cuore aveva completamente smesso di battere.

E senza mai alzare lo sguardo per scoprire da dove provenisse…

Allarme. Caddi a testa in giù, privo di sensi, sul corpo del mio.

Compagno caduto in battaglia.



Mi ritrovai, al risveglio, nella cabina di una grande nave.

La nave baleniera [[motifs/ship|navicella]] (il “Penguin”) era diretta a Nantucket; c'erano diverse persone a bordo.

were standing over me, and Augustus, paler than [[motifs/death|death]], was busily

occupied in chafing my hands. Upon seeing me open my eyes, his

exclamations of gratitude and joy excited alternate laughter and

[[motifs/tears|tears]] from the rough-looking personages who were present. The

mystery of our being in existence was now soon explained. We had

been run down by the whaling-[[motifs/ship|ship]], which was close-hauled,

beating up to Nantucket with every sail she could venture to set,

and consequently running almost at right angles to our own

course. Several men were on the look-out forward, but did not

perceive our boat until it was an impossibility to avoid coming

in contact—their shouts of warning upon seeing us were what so

terribly alarmed me. The huge [[motifs/ship|ship]], I was told, rode immediately

over us with as much ease as our own little vessel would have

passed over a feather, and without the least perceptible

impediment to her progress. Not a scream arose from the deck of

the victim—there was a slight grating sound to be heard mingling

with the roar of [[motifs/wind|wind]] and [[motifs/water|water]], as the frail bark which was

swallowed up rubbed for a moment along the keel of her

destroyer—but this was all. Thinking our boat (which it will be

remembered was dismasted) some mere shell cut adrift as useless,

the captain (Captain E. T. V. Block, of New [[settings/london|London]]) was for

proceeding on his course without troubling himself further about

the matter. Luckily, there were two of the look-out who swore

positively to having seen some person at our helm, and

represented the possibility of yet saving him. A discussion

ensued, when Block grew angry, and, after a while, said that “it

was no business of his to be eternally watching for egg-shells;

that the [[motifs/ship|ship]] should not put about for any such nonsense; and if

there was a man run down, it was nobody’s fault but his own, he

might drown and be dammed” or some language to that effect.

Henderson, the first mate, now took the matter up, being justly

indignant, as [[motifs/well|well]] as the whole [[motifs/ship|ship]]’s crew, at a speech evincing

so base a degree of heartless atrocity. He spoke plainly, seeing

himself upheld by the men, told the captain he considered him a

fit subject for the gallows, and that he would disobey his orders

if he were hanged for it the moment he set his foot on shore. He

strode aft, jostling Block (who turned pale and made no answer)

on one side, and seizing the helm, gave the word, in a firm

voice, Hard-a-lee! The men flew to their posts, and the [[motifs/ship|ship]] went

cleverly about. All this had occupied nearly five minutes, and it

was supposed to be hardly within the bounds of possibility that

any individual could be saved—allowing any to have been on board

the boat. Yet, as the reader has seen, both Augustus and myself

were rescued; and our deliverance seemed to have been brought

about by two of those almost inconceivable pieces of good fortune

which are attributed by the wise and pious to the special

interference of [[concepts/providence|Providence]].



While the [[motifs/ship|ship]] was yet in stays, the mate lowered the jolly-boat

and jumped into her with the very two men, I believe, who spoke

up as having seen me at the helm. They had just left the lee of

the vessel (the [[motifs/moon|moon]] still shining brightly) when she made a long

and heavy roll to windward, and Henderson, at the same moment,

starting up in his seat bawled out to his crew to back [[motifs/water|water]]. He

would say nothing else—repeating his cry impatiently, back [[motifs/water|water]]!

back [[motifs/water|water]]! The men put back as speedily as possible, but by this

[[motifs/time|time]] the [[motifs/ship|ship]] had gone round, and gotten fully under headway,

although all hands on board were making great exertions to take

in sail. In despite of the danger of the attempt, the mate clung

to the main-[[motifs/chains|chains]] as soon as they came within his reach. Another

huge lurch now brought the starboard side of the vessel out of

[[motifs/water|water]] nearly as far as her keel, when the cause of his anxiety

was rendered obvious enough. The [[concepts/body|body]] of a man was seen to be

affixed in the most singular manner to the smooth and shining

[[characters/bottom|bottom]] (the Penguin was coppered and copper-fastened), and

beating violently against it with every movement of the hull.

After several ineffectual efforts, made during the lurches of the

[[motifs/ship|ship]], and at the imminent risk of swamping the boat I was finally

disengaged from my perilous situation and taken on board—for the

[[concepts/body|body]] proved to be my own. It appeared that one of the

timber-bolts having started and broken a passage through the

copper, it had arrested my progress as I passed under the [[motifs/ship|ship]],

and fastened me in so extraordinary a manner to her [[characters/bottom|bottom]]. The

head of the bolt had made its way through the collar of the green

baize jacket I had on, and through the back part of my neck,

forcing itself out between two sinews and just below the right

ear. I was immediately put to bed—although life seemed to be

totally extinct. There was no surgeon on board. The captain,

however, treated me with every attention—to make amends, I

presume, in the eyes of his crew, for his atrocious behaviour in

the previous portion of the adventure.



In the meantime, Henderson had again put off from the [[motifs/ship|ship]],

although the [[motifs/wind|wind]] was now blowing almost a hurricane. He had not

been gone many minutes when he fell in with some fragments of our

Erano tutti in piedi sopra di me, e Augusto, più pallido della [[motifs/death|morte]], era molto impegnato.

“Occupato a strofinarmi le mani… Non appena mi ha visto aprire gli occhi…”

Esclamazioni di gratitudine e gioia suscitavano risate alternate…

[[motifs/tears|lacrime]] scesero dagli occhi di quei personaggi dall'aspetto rude che erano presenti.

Il mistero della nostra esistenza stava per essere finalmente spiegato… Noi avevamo…

Aveva stato investito dalla nave baleniera, che si trovava a distanza ravvicinata.

"Salpare verso Nantucket con tutte le vele disponibili"...

E di conseguenza, corre quasi perpendicolarmente rispetto al nostro percorso.

Nessuno in vista

Percepire la nostra barca fino al momento in cui diventa impossibile evitarne l’impatto…

In contatto: furono i loro gridi d’allarme nel vederci ad attirare la nostra attenzione.

Mi allarmò terribilmente. Quel enorme [[motifs/ship|navio]], mi dissero, si mosse immediatamente.

Che ci piombi addosso con la stessa facilità con cui potrebbe farlo anche la nostra piccola imbarcazione…

Trascorso inosservato… e senza il minimo segno evidente

Un ostacolo al suo progresso… Nessun grido provenne dal ponte…

La vittima… si udiva un leggero suono stridulo che si mescolava al resto…

Con il ruggito del [[motifs/wind|vento]] e dell’[[motifs/water|acqua]], mentre quella fragile barca.

Tragata via… sfregata per un momento lungo la carena di lei

Distruttore… ma era tutto ciò che c’era. Pensavamo che la nostra barca fosse al sicuro… ma non lo era.

“Ricordato… ma senza alberi; soltanto un guscio inutile, alla deriva.”

Il capitano (il Capitano E. T. V. Block, di New [[settings/london|Londra]]) era a favore.

Proseguire per la propria strada senza preoccuparsi ulteriormente di…

La questione… Fortunatamente, c’erano due di quei sentinelli che giurarono…

Con grande soddisfazione nel vedere che c’è qualcuno al comando…

"Rappresentava la possibilità di salvarlo ancora… Una discussione."

Successivamente, quando Block si arrabbiò e, dopo un po’, disse che “era…”.

Non spettava a lui stare continuamente attento a eventuali “gusci d’uovo”.

Che la [[motifs/ship|nave]] non dovesse intraprendere nulla del genere; e se.

C’era un uomo che era stato investito… Non era colpa di nessuno, se non sua.

“Potrebbe annegare e finire intrappolato nella diga”, o qualcosa del genere.

Henderson, il primo ufficiale, prese in mano la questione, poiché era giusto farlo

Indignati, proprio come l'intero equipaggio della[[motifs/ship|nave]], di fronte a un discorso che rivelava.

Una bassezza tale da raggiungere livelli di atrocità senza cuore. Parlava con franchezza, consapevole di ciò che stava dicendo.

“Sostenuto dagli uomini intorno a lui, disse al capitano di considerarlo…”

Un individuo degno della forca, che si rifiuta di obbedire ai suoi ordini.

Se fosse stato impiccato non appena avesse messo piede sulla riva…

“Camminò deciso verso poppa, spingendo Block, che impallidì e non rispose nulla.”

Da un lato… e prendendo il timone, diede l’ordine con fermezza.

“Voce. Hard-a-lee!” Gli uomini si precipitarono ai loro posti, e la [[motifs/ship|nave]] partì immediatamente.

Qualsiasi individuo potrebbe essere salvato… il che significa che chiunque potesse trovarsi a bordo sarebbe stato in grado di salvarsi.

Il barca… Eppure, come il lettore ha potuto notare, sia Augustus che io stesso…

Furono salvati; e sembrava che la nostra liberazione fosse finalmente arrivata

Con due di quei casi fortunati quasi inimmaginabili

Quelli che i saggi e i devoti attribuiscono alle caratteristiche particolari…

Intervento della [[concepts/providence|Provvidenza]].

E saltarono dentro insieme a quei due uomini che, credo, avevano parlato prima…

Alzati in piedi, come se mi avessero visto al timone… Avevano appena lasciato la protezione dell’albero di maestra…

La nave (la [[motifs/moon|luna]] che ancora brillava intensamente) quando fece un lungo viaggio.

E un forte rollio verso il lato ventoso… e in quel stesso momento, Henderson…

Non avrebbe detto nulla altro: ripeteva impazientemente il suo grido, “Torna indietro nell’[[motifs/water|acqua]]!”

Indietro verso l’[[motifs/water|acqua]]! Gli uomini si misero in movimento il più rapidamente possibile, ma ormai.

Dopo che la [[motifs/ship|nave]] aveva completato il giro e iniziato a muoversi a tutta velocità,

Nonostante tutti a bordo si stessero impegnando al massimo per riuscirci…

Attaccato in modo davvero unico alla superficie liscia e lucida

Dopo diversi tentativi falliti, effettuati durante i momenti di incertezza…

La [[motifs/ship|barca]], e con il rischio imminente di farla allagare, finalmente.

Il [[concepts/body|corpo]] risultò essere il mio stesso. Sembrava che uno dei.

Cannoni di legno che hanno iniziato a rompere la strada attraverso…

Il rame, aveva ostacolato il mio avanzamento mentre passavo sotto la [[motifs/ship|nave]].

E mi fissò in modo così straordinario alla sua [[characters/bottom|parte inferiore]].

Forzandosi a uscire tra due tendini, appena sotto il lato destro…

Subito messo a letto… anche se la vita sembrava…

Del tutto estinto… Non c’era nessun chirurgo a bordo… Il capitano…

Comunque, mi ha trattato con grande attenzione… per fare ammenda.

Si presume, agli occhi del suo equipaggio, a causa del suo comportamento atroce…

La parte precedente dell’avventura.

Nonostante il [[motifs/wind|vento]] soffiasse ormai con la forza di un uragano, lui non si era mosso.

Sono passati molti minuti quando si è imbattuto in alcuni frammenti dei nostri…



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_01--part_04" data-title="The Narrative of A. Gordon Pym (Raven Edition) — Chapter 1 (part 4)" data-chapter="Chapter 01" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="motif/clock,motif/death,motif/nature,motif/night,motif/ship,motif/time,motif/water,motif/wind,concept/deception,concept/despair,concept/doubt,concept/freedom,concept/nature,setting/ship,character/ariel"></span>


boat, and shortly afterward one of the men with him asserted that

he could distinguish a cry for help at intervals amid the roaring

of the tempest. This induced the hardy seamen to persevere in

their search for more than half an hour, although repeated

signals to return were made them by Captain Block, and although

every moment on the [[motifs/water|water]] in so frail a boat was fraught to them

with the most imminent and deadly peril. Indeed, it is nearly

impossible to conceive how the small jolly they were in could

have escaped destruction for a single instant. She was built,

however, for the whaling service, and was fitted, as I have since

had reason to believe, with air-boxes, in the manner of some

life-boats used on the coast of Wales.



After searching in vain for about the period of [[motifs/time|time]] just

mentioned, it was determined to get back to the [[motifs/ship|ship]]. They had

scarcely made this resolve when a feeble cry arose from a dark

object that floated rapidly by. They pursued and soon overtook

it. It proved to be the entire deck of the [[characters/ariel|Ariel]]’s cuddy.

Augustus was struggling near it, apparently in the last agonies.

Upon getting hold of him it was found that he was attached by a

rope to the floating timber. This rope, it will be remembered, I

had myself tied around his waist, and made fast to a ringbolt,

for the purpose of keeping him in an upright position, and my so

doing, it appeared, had been ultimately the means of preserving

his life. The [[characters/ariel|Ariel]] was slightly put together, and in going down

her frame naturally went to pieces; the deck of the cuddy, as

might have been expected, was lifted, by the force of the [[motifs/water|water]]

rushing in, entirely from the main timbers, and floated (with

other fragments, no [[concepts/doubt|doubt]]) to the surface—Augustus was buoyed up

with it, and thus escaped a terrible [[motifs/death|death]].



It was more than an hour after being taken on board the Penguin

before he could give any account of himself, or be made to

comprehend the [[concepts/nature|nature]] of the accident which had befallen our

boat. At length he became thoroughly aroused, and spoke much of

his sensations while in the [[motifs/water|water]]. Upon his first attaining any

degree of consciousness, he found himself beneath the surface,

whirling round and round with inconceivable rapidity, and with a

rope wrapped in three or four folds tightly about his neck. In an

instant afterward he felt himself going rapidly upward, when, his

head striking violently against a hard substance, he again

relapsed into insensibility. Upon once more reviving he was in

fuller possession of his reason—this was still, however, in the

greatest degree clouded and confused. He now knew that some

accident had occurred, and that he was in the [[motifs/water|water]], although his

mouth was above the surface, and he could breathe with some

[[concepts/freedom|freedom]]. Possibly, at this period the deck was drifting rapidly

before the [[motifs/wind|wind]], and drawing him after it, as he floated upon his

back. Of course, as long as he could have retained this position,

it would have been nearly impossible that he should be drowned.

Presently a surge threw him directly athwart the deck, and this

post he endeavored to maintain, screaming at intervals for help.

Just before he was discovered by Mr. Henderson, he had been

obliged to relax his hold through exhaustion, and, falling into

the sea, had given himself up for lost. During the whole period

of his struggles he had not the faintest recollection of the

[[characters/ariel|Ariel]], nor of the matters in connexion with the source of his

disaster. A vague feeling of terror and [[concepts/despair|despair]] had taken entire

possession of his faculties. When he was finally picked up, every

power of his mind had failed him; and, as before said, it was

nearly an hour after getting on board the Penguin before he

became fully aware of his condition. In regard to myself—I was

resuscitated from a state bordering very nearly upon [[motifs/death|death]] (and

after every other means had been tried in vain for three hours

and a half) by vigorous friction with flannels bathed in hot

oil—a proceeding suggested by Augustus. The wound in my neck,

although of an ugly appearance, proved of little real

consequence, and I soon recovered from its effects.



The Penguin got into port about nine o’[[motifs/clock|clock]] in the morning,

after encountering one of the severest gales ever experienced off

Nantucket. Both Augustus and myself managed to appear at Mr.

Barnard’s in [[motifs/time|time]] for breakfast—which, luckily, was somewhat

late, owing to the party over [[motifs/night|night]]. I suppose all at the table

were too much fatigued themselves to notice our jaded

appearance—of course, it would not have borne a very rigid

scrutiny. Schoolboys, however, can accomplish wonders in the way

of [[concepts/deception|deception]], and I verily believe not one of our friends in

Nantucket had the slightest suspicion that the terrible story

told by some sailors in town of their having run down a vessel at

sea and drowned some thirty or forty poor devils, had reference

either to the [[characters/ariel|Ariel]], my companion, or myself. We two have since

very frequently talked the matter over—but never without a

shudder. In one of our conversations Augustus frankly confessed

to me, that in his whole life he had at no [[motifs/time|time]] experienced so

excruciating a sense of dismay, as when on board our little boat

he first discovered the extent of his intoxication, and felt

himself sinking beneath its influence.

Barca… e poco dopo uno degli uomini con lui affermò che

Un grido d’aiuto che si udiva di tanto in tanto tra il fragore assordante…

Della tempesta. Questo incoraggiò i marinai coraggiosi a perseverare.

La loro ricerca è durata più di mezz’ora, nonostante sia stata ripetuta più volte.

Il Capitano Block inviò dei segnali per farli tornare indietro, e nonostante ciò…

Ogni momento trascorso sull’[[motifs/water|acqua]], in una barca così fragile, era per loro pieno di pericoli.

Con il pericolo più imminente e mortale… Infatti, è quasi inevitabile.

Non si può nemmeno immaginare quanto fossero felici…

Solo per un istante è riuscita a sfuggire alla distruzione… Fu costruita…

Tuttavia, per il servizio di caccia alle balene, fu attrezzato così come lo è stato da allora.

Aveva motivo di credere, con certe prove concrete, che fosse così…

Barche di salvataggio utilizzate sulla costa del Galles.



Dopo aver cercato invano per circa quel lasso di [[motifs/time|tempo]], alla fine.

Come già accennato, fu deciso di tornare sull’[[motifs/ship|nave]]. Loro avevano.

Appena presi questa decisione, un debole grido provenne dall’oscurità…

Oggetto che fluttuava rapidamente… Lo inseguirono e presto lo raggiunsero.

Si rivelò essere l'intero mazzo di carte del cestino di [[characters/ariel|Ariel]].

Augusto lottava vicino ad esso, chiaramente nelle sue ultime sofferenze.

Quando lo trovarono, si scoprì che era legato con…

“Corda legata al tronco galleggiante… Questa corda, come si ricorderà, io…”

Mi ero legata intorno alla sua vita e l’avevo fissata a un anello di ferro.

Per il fine di mantenerlo in posizione eretta… e il mio…

A quanto pare, l’azione stessa era diventata il mezzo per preservare…

La sua vita. L’[[characters/ariel|Ariel]] era piuttosto in ordine, quando iniziò a scendere.

Il suo corpo, naturalmente, iniziò a distruggersi; il ponte della cabina…

Ciò che si poteva aspettare fu effettivamente realizzato, grazie alla forza dell’[[motifs/water|acqua]].

Titolo:  
“Entrando a tutta velocità, interamente formato dai tronchi principali, e fluttuando…”

Altri frammenti, senza alcun [[concepts/doubt|dubbio]], vennero alla luce; Augusto ne fu incoraggiato.

Grazie ad esso, riuscì così a sfuggire a una terribile [[motifs/death|morte]].



Passò più di un’ora dopo essere stato portato a bordo del “Penguin”.

Prima che potesse spiegarsi o essere interrogato…

Comprendere la [[concepts/nature|natura]] dell'incidente che ci è accaduto.

Finalmente si svegliò del tutto e parlò molto…

Le sue sensazioni mentre si trovava nell’[[motifs/water|acqua]]. La prima volta che riuscì a percepirle.

Livello di coscienza… si trovò sotto la superficie.

Rotando vorticosamente a una velocità inimmaginabile…

Una corda avvolta strettamente tre o quattro volte intorno al suo collo…

Immediatamente dopo, sentì di essere spinto verso l’alto con grande velocità…

La testa colpisce violentemente una superficie dura… ancora una volta

Ripiombò nell’incoscienza. Una volta ripreso i sensi, si trovava…

Una più completa padronanza della propria ragione… Questo, tuttavia, rimaneva ancora da realizzare.

Il suo stato d’animo era ora profondamente offuscato e confuso; sapeva ormai che qualcosa…

Un incidente era avvenuto, ed egli si trovava nell’[[motifs/water|acqua]], anche se.

La bocca era fuori dall’acqua, e poteva respirare liberamente.

[[concepts/freedom|libertà]]. Forse, in quel periodo, la nave stava galleggiando velocemente alla deriva.

Prima del [[motifs/wind|vento]], attirandolo con sé mentre fluttuava su di esso.

“Indietro”. Naturalmente, purché fosse riuscito a mantenere quella posizione…

Sarebbe stato quasi impossibile che annegasse.

In quel momento, una forte ondata lo scaraventò dritto sul ponte…

Dopo aver cercato in tutti i modi di mantenerla in piedi, gridava di tanto in tanto chiedendo aiuto.

Prima di essere scoperto dal signor Henderson, era stato…

Costretto a allentare la presa a causa dell’esaurimento, cadde…

Il mare sembrava essersi arreso alla sconfitta… Per tutto quel periodo.

Di quelle sue lotte, non aveva la minima memoria.

[[characters/ariel|Ariel]], né delle questioni relative alla fonte della sua esistenza.

Disastro. Un vago senso di terrore e [[concepts/despair|disperazione]] aveva invaso tutto.

La perdita delle proprie facoltà mentali… Quando finalmente fu ritrovato, ogni…

La forza della sua mente lo aveva abbandonato; e, come detto in precedenza, era…

Quasi un’ora dopo essere salito a bordo del “Penguin”, prima che…

Divenne pienamente consapevole della sua condizione. Per quanto riguarda me… ero…

Risuscitato da uno stato che quasi sfiorava la [[motifs/death|morte]] (e, )

Dopo che tutti gli altri metodi erano stati tentati invano per tre ore

E mezzo) attraverso una vigorosa frizione con panni imbevuti in acqua calda

Olio: una procedura suggerita da Augusto… La ferita sul mio collo…

Nonostante un aspetto brutto, si rivelò di poco valore reale

Di conseguenza, riuscii presto a riprendermi dai suoi effetti.



Il Pingüino arrivò in porto verso le nove di [[motifs/clock|ore]] del mattino.

Titolo:  
Dopo aver affrontato una delle tempeste più violente mai registrate al largo…

Nantucket. Sia Augustus che io riuscimmo ad apparire dal signor.

Barnard era in tempo per la colazione; fortunatamente, quella volta era abbastanza.

In ritardo, a causa della festa di quella [[motifs/night|notte]]. Immagino che tutti quelli seduti attorno al tavolo.

Erano troppo stanchi per notare la nostra apatia

Apparenza: ovviamente, non avrebbe potuto essere troppo rigida…

Esame attento. Tuttavia, i ragazzi possono compiere miracoli…

Di [[concepts/deception|inganno]]; e credo sinceramente che nessuno dei nostri amici.

Nantucket aveva la più vaga intuizione che quella terribile storia…

Raccontato da alcuni marinai della città di come abbiano affondato una nave…

Titolo:  
Il mare inghiottì circa trenta o quaranta poveri diavoli…

O a [[characters/ariel|Ariel]], la mia compagna, o a me stesso. Da allora, noi due.

Molto spesso ne discutevano, ma mai senza…

Shudder… In una delle nostre conversazioni, Augustus confessò francamente…

Per me, significa che in tutta la sua vita non aveva mai sperimentato nulla del genere.

Un senso di disperazione straziante, proprio come quando si è a bordo della nostra piccola barca…

Scoprì per la prima volta quanto fosse profondo il suo stato di ebbrezza, e ne ebbe consapevolezza

Lui stesso finiva per essere sopraffatto dal suo influsso.



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_02--part_01" data-title="The Narrative of A. Gordon Pym (Raven Edition) — Chapter 2 (part 1)" data-chapter="Chapter 02" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="motif/death,motif/desire,motif/memory,motif/night,motif/tears,motif/time,motif/well,concept/deception,concept/despair,concept/imagination,concept/longing,concept/melancholy,concept/suffering,character/ariel"></span>


CHAPTER 2





In no affairs of mere prejudice, pro or con, do we deduce

inferences with entire certainty, even from the most simple data.

It might be supposed that a catastrophe such as I have just

related would have effectually cooled my incipient passion for

the sea. On the contrary, I never experienced a more ardent

[[concepts/longing|longing]] for the wild adventures incident to the life of a

navigator than within a week after our miraculous deliverance.

This short period proved amply long enough to erase from my

[[motifs/memory|memory]] the shadows, and bring out in vivid light all the

pleasurably exciting points of color, all the picturesqueness, of

the late perilous accident. My conversations with Augustus grew

daily more frequent and more intensely full of interest. He had a

manner of relating his stories of the ocean (more than one half

of which I now suspect to have been sheer fabrications) [[motifs/well|well]]

adapted to have weight with one of my enthusiastic temperament

and somewhat gloomy although glowing [[concepts/imagination|imagination]]. It is strange,

too, that he most strongly enlisted my feelings in behalf of the

life of a seaman, when he depicted his more terrible moments of

[[concepts/suffering|suffering]] and [[concepts/despair|despair]]. For the bright side of the painting I had

a limited sympathy. My visions were of shipwreck and famine; of

[[motifs/death|death]] or captivity among barbarian hordes; of a lifetime dragged

out in sorrow and [[motifs/tears|tears]], upon some gray and desolate rock, in an

ocean unapproachable and unknown. Such visions or desires—for

they amounted to desires—are common, I have since been assured,

to the whole numerous race of the [[concepts/melancholy|melancholy]] among men—at the

[[motifs/time|time]] of which I speak I regarded them only as prophetic glimpses

of a destiny which I felt myself in a measure bound to fulfil.

Augustus thoroughly entered into my state of mind. It is

probable, indeed, that our intimate communion had resulted in a

partial interchange of character.



About eighteen months after the period of the [[characters/ariel|Ariel]]’s disaster,

the firm of Lloyd and Vredenburgh (a [[house]] connected in some

manner with the Messieurs Enderby, I believe, of Liverpool) were

engaged in repairing and fitting out the brig Grampus for a

whaling voyage. She was an old hulk, and scarcely seaworthy when

all was done to her that could be done. I hardly know why she was

chosen in preference to other good vessels belonging to the same

owners—but so it was. Mr. Barnard was appointed to command her,

and Augustus was going with him. While the brig was getting

ready, he frequently urged upon me the excellency of the

opportunity now offered for indulging my [[motifs/desire|desire]] of travel. He

found me by no means an unwilling listener—yet the matter could

not be so easily arranged. My father made no direct opposition;

but my mother went into hysterics at the bare mention of the

design; and, more than all, my grandfather, from whom I expected

much, vowed to cut me off with a shilling if I should ever broach

the subject to him again. These difficulties, however, so far

from abating my [[motifs/desire|desire]], only added fuel to the flame. I

determined to go at all hazards; and, having made known my

intentions to Augustus, we set about arranging a plan by which it

might be accomplished. In the meantime I forbore speaking to any

of my relations in regard to the voyage, and, as I busied myself

ostensibly with my usual studies, it was supposed that I had

abandoned the design. I have since frequently examined my conduct

on this occasion with sentiments of displeasure as [[motifs/well|well]] as of

surprise. The intense hypocrisy I made use of for the furtherance

of my project—an hypocrisy pervading every word and action of my

life for so long a period of [[motifs/time|time]]—could only have been rendered

tolerable to myself by the wild and burning expectation with

which I looked forward to the fulfilment of my long-cherished

visions of travel.



In pursuance of my scheme of [[concepts/deception|deception]], I was necessarily obliged

to leave much to the management of Augustus, who was employed for

the greater part of every day on board the Grampus, attending to

some arrangements for his father in the cabin and cabin hold. At

[[motifs/night|night]], however, we were sure to have a conference and talk over

our hopes. After nearly a month passed in this manner, without

our hitting upon any plan we thought likely to succeed, he told

me at last that he had determined upon everything necessary. I

had a relation living in New Bedford, a Mr. Ross, at whose [[house]]

I was in the habit of spending occasionally two or three weeks at

a [[motifs/time|time]]. The brig was to sail about the middle of June (June,

1827), and it was agreed that, a day or two before her putting to

sea, my father was to receive a note, as usual, from Mr. Ross,

asking me to come over and spend a fortnight with Robert and

Emmet (his sons). Augustus charged himself with the inditing of

this note and getting it delivered. Having set out as supposed,

for New Bedford, I was then to report myself to my companion, who

would contrive a hiding-place for me in the Grampus. This

hiding-place, he assured me, would be rendered sufficiently

comfortable for a residence of many days, during which I was not

to make my appearance. When the brig had proceeded so far on her

course as to make any turning back a matter out of question, I

should then, he said, be formally installed in all the comforts

CAPITOLO 2





In nessun caso basato semplicemente su pregiudizi, né a favore né contro, traiamo conclusioni

Inferenze possibili con assoluta certezza, anche a partire dai dati più semplici.

Si potrebbe pensare che una catastrofe del genere…

Titolo:  
“Relato” avrebbe effettivamente spento la mia nascente passione per…

Il mare… Al contrario, non ho mai vissuto un’esperienza più appassionata.

[[concepts/longing|Desiderio]] per le avventure selvagge che fanno parte della vita di.

Un navigatore migliore di chiunque altro entro una settimana dopo il nostro miracoloso salvataggio.

Questo breve periodo si rivelò più che sufficiente per cancellare dalla mia memoria…

[[motifs/memory|Ricordare]] le ombre, e far emergere alla luce vivida tutto ciò.

Titolo:  
Punti di colore piacevolmente emozionanti, tutta quella pittoresca bellezza…

L’incidente pericoloso avvenuto in un momento critico… Le mie conversazioni con Augustus si sono intensificate.

Ogni giorno diventava sempre più frequente e intensamente interessante… Lui aveva…

Modo di raccontare le sue storie sull’oceano (più della metà)

Di cui ora sospetto che siano state pura invenzione.

Adattato per esprimere il peso e l’entusiasmo del mio carattere.

Era piuttosto cupo, nonostante un’[[concepts/imagination|immaginazione]] vivida. È strano.

Anche lui fece sì che i miei sentimenti si schierassero con forza dalla sua parte

La vita di un marinaio: i suoi momenti più terribili descritti in dettaglio

[[concepts/suffering|sofferenza]] e [[concepts/despair|disperazione]]. Ma per il lato positivo di questa situazione, avevo.

Una compassione limitata… Le mie visioni riguardavano naufragi e carestie; di…

[[motifs/death|morte]] o prigionia tra le orde barbare; una vita trascorsa in condizioni disumane.

Fuori, nel dolore e tra le [[motifs/tears|lacrime]], su qualche roccia grigia e desolata.

Oceano inaccessibile e sconosciuto… Tali visioni o desideri…

Desideri comuni…

A tutta quella numerosa razza di persone melanconiche tra gli uomini.

Nel periodo di cui parlo, li consideravo soltanto come anticipazioni profetiche.

Di un destino che sentivo di dover, in qualche modo, realizzare.

“Augustus ha completamente compreso il mio stato d’animo… È così.”

Probabilmente, infatti, la nostra intima condivisione abbia portato a…

Scambio parziale dei caratteri.



Circa diciotto mesi dopo il periodo del disastro di [[characters/ariel|Ariel]],

La società Lloyd and Vredenburgh, un’[[house|azienda]] collegata in qualche modo.

Credo che il modo in cui i signori Enderby di Liverpool si comportassero…

Occupati nella riparazione e nell’equipaggiamento della brigata Grampus per…

Viaggio di caccia alle balene. Era una vecchia carcassa, a malapena idonea a navigare…

Tutto ciò che era possibile farle le fu fatto… Non so proprio perché lei fosse…

Scelto preferibilmente ad altri buoni vasi appartenenti allo stesso…

I proprietari… ma era proprio così. Il signor Barnard fu incaricato di comandarla.

E Augusto lo accompagnava… Mentre la brigata si preparava…

Pronto, mi ripeteva spesso quanto fosse eccellente…

Ora c'è l'opportunità di soddisfare il mio desiderio di viaggiare. Lui.

Non mi ha certo trovato un ascoltatore riluttante… tuttavia, la questione poteva comunque essere discussa.

Non è così facile sistemare le cose. Mio padre non ebbe alcuna obiezione diretta…

Ma mia madre andò nel panico appena menzionato…

Design… e, soprattutto, mio nonno, da cui mi aspettavo molto.

“Much… promiseva di tagliarmi i fondi se mai avessi osato menzionarlo.”

Il soggetto torna di nuovo davanti a lui… Tuttavia, queste difficoltà, per il momento…

Invece di attenuare il mio [[motifs/desire|desiderio]], ha solo alimentato ancora di più la fiamma. Io.

Deciso a correre tutti i rischi possibili; e, dopo averne fatto conoscenza…

Con l’intento di agire secondo le indicazioni di Augusto, ci mettemmo all’opera per elaborare un piano concreto.

Potrebbe essere realizzato… Nel frattempo, ho deciso di non parlare con nessuno.

Titolo:  
Delle mie relazioni riguardo al viaggio, e mentre mi occupavo di…

In apparenza, impegnato come al solito nei miei studi, si pensava che io fossi…

Abbandonai quel progetto. Da allora ho spesso riflettuto sul mio comportamento.

In questa occasione, con sentimenti di disappunto tanto quanto.

Sorpresa: L’ipocrisia intensa che ho utilizzato per proseguire…

L’ipocrisia che permea ogni parola e azione del mio progetto

La vita, per un periodo così lungo di [[motifs/time|tempo]], poteva essere vissuta solo in questo modo.

“Tollerabile per me, grazie all’aspettativa ardente e intensa…”

A cui aspettavo con ansia l’attuazione del mio desiderio più caro

Visioni di viaggio.



Al fine di attuare il mio piano di [[concepts/deception|inganno]], ero necessariamente costretto a farlo.

Lasciare gran parte delle decisioni al management di Augusto, che era incaricato di gestirle.

La maggior parte della giornata a bordo del Grampus, dedicata alle…

Alcuni accordi per suo padre nella cabina e nel vano di stiva.

Tuttavia, di [[motifs/night|notte]], eravamo sicuri che avremmo tenuto una riunione per discuterne.

Le nostre speranze… Dopo quasi un mese trascorso in questo modo, senza…

Non appena trovavamo un piano che ritenevamo potesse avere successo, lui lo proponeva immediatamente.

Finalmente, aveva deciso di fare tutto ciò che era necessario. Io…

Aveva una relazione con un signore che viveva a New Bedford, il signor Ross; era nella sua [[house|casa]].

Trascorrevo spesso due o tre settimane…

A [[motifs/time|quell’epoca]]. La brigata avrebbe dovuto salpare verso metà giugno. Giugno.

1827, e fu concordato che, uno o due giorni prima della sua partenza…

Mare… Mio padre avrebbe ricevuto, come al solito, una lettera da parte del signor Ross.

“Chiedendomi di venire a trascorrere quindici giorni con Robert…”

Emmet (i suoi figli). Augustus si incaricò personalmente della stesura…

“Questa nota e il suo consegno… Dopo essere partiti come previsto…”

Per New Bedford, dovevo poi presentarmi al mio compagno…

“Troverebbe un nascondiglio per me sul Grampus…”

“Un nascondiglio”, mi assicurò, sarebbe stato sufficientemente sicuro…

Adatto a un soggiorno di molti giorni… durante i quali, però, non lo fui.

Per farsi vedere… Quando la brigantina aveva già percorso una certa distanza…

Per evitare qualsiasi possibilità di ritorno, decisi con fermezza…

“Allora, disse, dovrebbe essere formalmente insediato in tutte le comodità disponibili.”



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_02--part_02" data-title="The Narrative of A. Gordon Pym (Raven Edition) — Chapter 2 (part 2)" data-chapter="Chapter 02" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="motif/home,motif/nature,motif/rose,motif/soul,motif/time,motif/water,motif/well,concept/nature,character/edmund"></span>


of the cabin; and as to his father, he would only laugh heartily

at the joke. Vessels enough would be met with by which a letter

might be sent [[motifs/home|home]] explaining the adventure to my parents.



The middle of June at length arrived, and every thing had been

matured. The note was written and delivered, and on a Monday

morning I left the [[house]] for the New Bedford packet, as supposed.

I went, however, straight to Augustus, who was waiting for me at

the corner of a street. It had been our original plan that I

should keep out of the way until dark, and then slip on board the

brig; but, as there was now a thick fog in our favor, it was

agreed to lose no [[motifs/time|time]] in secreting me. Augustus led the way to

the wharf, and I followed at a little distance, enveloped in a

thick seaman’s cloak, which he had brought with him, so that my

person might not be easily recognized. Just as we turned the

second corner, after passing Mr. [[characters/edmund|Edmund]]’s [[motifs/well|well]], who should

appear, standing right in front of me, and looking me full in the

face, but old Mr. Peterson, my grandfather. “Why, bless my [[motifs/soul|soul]],

Gordon,” said he, after a long pause, “why, why,—whose dirty

cloak is that you have on?” “Sir!” I replied, assuming, as [[motifs/well|well]]

as I could, in the exigency of the moment, an air of offended

surprise, and talking in the gruffest of all imaginable

tones—“sir! you are a sum’mat mistaken—my name, in the first

place, bee’nt nothing at all like Goddin, and I’d want you for to

know better, you blackguard, than to call my new obercoat a darty

one.” For my life I could hardly refrain from screaming with

laughter at the odd manner in which the old gentleman received

this handsome rebuke. He started back two or three steps, turned

first pale and then excessively red, threw up his spectacles,

then, putting them down, ran full tilt at me, with his umbrella

uplifted. He stopped short, however, in his career, as if struck

with a sudden recollection; and presently, turning round, hobbled

off down the street, shaking all the while with rage, and

muttering between his teeth: “Won’t do—new glasses—thought it was

Gordon—d—d good-for-nothing salt [[motifs/water|water]] Long Tom.”



After this narrow escape we proceeded with greater caution, and

arrived at our point of destination in safety. There were only

one or two of the hands on board, and these were busy forward,

doing something to the forecastle combings. Captain Barnard, we

knew very [[motifs/well|well]], was engaged at Lloyd and Vredenburgh’s, and would

remain there until late in the evening, so we had little to

apprehend on his account. Augustus went first up the vessel’s

side, and in a short while I followed him, without being noticed

by the men at work. We proceeded at once into the cabin, and

found no person there. It was fitted up in the most comfortable

style—a thing somewhat unusual in a whaling-vessel. There were

four very excellent staterooms, with wide and convenient berths.

There was also a large stove, I took notice, and a remarkably

thick and valuable carpet covering the floor of both the cabin

and staterooms. The ceiling was full seven feet high, and, in

short, every thing appeared of a more roomy and agreeable [[concepts/nature|nature]]

than I had anticipated. Augustus, however, would allow me but

little [[motifs/time|time]] for observation, insisting upon the necessity of my

concealing myself as soon as possible. He led the way into his

own stateroom, which was on the starboard side of the brig, and

next to the bulkheads. Upon entering, he closed the door and

bolted it. I thought I had never seen a nicer little room than

the one in which I now found myself. It was about ten feet long,

and had only one berth, which, as I said before, was wide and

convenient. In that portion of the closet nearest the bulkheads

there was a space of four feet square, containing a table, a

chair, and a set of hanging shelves full of books, chiefly books

of voyages and travels. There were many other little comforts in

the room, among which I ought not to forget a kind of safe or

refrigerator, in which Augustus pointed out to me a host of

delicacies, both in the eating and drinking department.



He now pressed with his knuckles upon a certain spot of the

carpet in one corner of the space just mentioned, letting me know

that a portion of the flooring, about sixteen inches square, had

been neatly cut out and again adjusted. As he pressed, this

portion [[motifs/rose|rose]] up at one end sufficiently to allow the passage of

his finger beneath. In this manner he raised the mouth of the

trap (to which the carpet was still fastened by tacks), and I

found that it led into the after hold. He next lit a small taper

by means of a phosphorous match, and, placing the light in a dark

lantern, descended with it through the opening, bidding me

follow. I did so, and he then pulled the cover upon the hole, by

means of a nail driven into the under side—the carpet, of course,

resuming its original position on the floor of the stateroom, and

all traces of the aperture being concealed.



The taper gave out so feeble a ray that it was with the greatest

difficulty I could grope my way through the confused mass of

lumber among which I now found myself. By degrees, however, my

eyes became accustomed to the gloom, and I proceeded with less

trouble, holding on to the skirts of my friend’s coat. He brought

me, at length, after creeping and winding through innumerable
