<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_17--part_01" data-title="The Narrative of A. Gordon Pym (Raven Edition) — Chapter 17 (part 1)" data-chapter="Chapter 17" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="motif/birds,motif/noon,motif/snow,motif/water,motif/well,motif/wind,concept/doubt,concept/hope,setting/mountains,setting/new_york"></span>


CHAPTER 17





We kept our course southwardly for four days after giving up the

search for Glass’s islands, without meeting with any ice at all.

On the twenty-sixth, at [[motifs/noon|noon]], we were in latitude 63 degrees 23’

S., longitude 41 degrees 25’ W. We now saw several large ice

islands, and a floe of field ice, not, however, of any great

extent. The winds generally blew from the southeast, or the

northeast, but were very light. Whenever we had a westerly [[motifs/wind|wind]],

which was seldom, it was invariably attended with a rain squall.

Every day we had more or less [[motifs/snow|snow]]. The thermometer, on the

twenty-seventh stood at thirty-five.



January 1, 1828.—This day we found ourselves completely hemmed in

by the ice, and our prospects looked cheerless indeed. A strong

gale blew, during the whole forenoon, from the northeast, and

drove large cakes of the drift against the rudder and counter

with such violence that we all trembled for the consequences.

Toward evening, the gale still blowing with fury, a large field

in front separated, and we were enabled, by carrying a press of

sail to force a passage through the smaller flakes into some open

[[motifs/water|water]] beyond. As we approached this space we took in sail by

degrees, and having at length got clear, lay-to under a single

reefed foresail.



January 2.—We had now tolerably pleasant weather. At [[motifs/noon|noon]] we

found ourselves in latitude 69 degrees 10’ S, longitude 42

degrees 20’ W, having crossed the Antarctic circle. Very little

ice was to be seen to the southward, although large fields of it

lay behind us. This day we rigged some sounding gear, using a

large iron pot capable of holding twenty gallons, and a line of

two hundred fathoms. We found the current setting to the north,

about a quarter of a mile per hour. The temperature of the air

was now about thirty-three. Here we found the variation to be 14

degrees 28’ easterly, per azimuth.



January 5.—We had still held on to the southward without any very

great impediments. On this morning, however, being in latitude 73

degrees 15’ E., longitude 42 degrees 10’ W, we were again brought

to a stand by an immense expanse of firm ice. We saw,

nevertheless, much open [[motifs/water|water]] to the southward, and felt no [[concepts/doubt|doubt]]

of being able to reach it eventually. Standing to the eastward

along the edge of the floe, we at length came to a passage of

about a mile in width, through which we warped our way by

sundown. The sea in which we now were was thickly covered with

ice islands, but had no field ice, and we pushed on boldly as

before. The cold did not seem to increase, although we had [[motifs/snow|snow]]

very frequently, and now and then hail squalls of great violence.

Immense flocks of the albatross flew over the schooner this day,

going from southeast to northwest.



January 7.—The sea still remained pretty [[motifs/well|well]] open, so that we

had no difficulty in holding on our course. To the westward we

saw some icebergs of incredible size, and in the afternoon passed

very near one whose summit could not have been less than four

hundred fathoms from the surface of the ocean. Its girth was

probably, at the base, three-quarters of a league, and several

streams of [[motifs/water|water]] were running from crevices in its sides. We

remained in sight of this island two days, and then only lost it

in a fog.



January 10.—Early this morning we had the misfortune to lose a

man overboard. He was an American named Peter Vredenburgh, a

native of [[settings/new-york|New York]], and was one of the most valuable hands on

board the schooner. In going over the bows his foot slipped, and

he fell between two cakes of ice, never rising again. At [[motifs/noon|noon]] of

this day we were in latitude 78 degrees 30’, longitude 40 degrees

15’ W. The cold was now excessive, and we had hail squalls

continually from the northward and eastward. In this direction

also we saw several more immense icebergs, and the whole horizon

to the eastward appeared to be blocked up with field ice, rising

in tiers, one mass above the other. Some driftwood floated by

during the evening, and a great quantity of [[motifs/birds|birds]] flew over,

among which were nellies, peterels, albatrosses, and a large bird

of a brilliant blue plumage. The variation here, per azimuth, was

less than it had been previously to our passing the Antarctic

circle.



January 12.—Our passage to the south again looked doubtful, as

nothing was to be seen in the direction of the pole but one

apparently limitless floe, backed by absolute [[settings/mountains|mountains]] of ragged

ice, one precipice of which arose frowningly above the other. We

stood to the westward until the fourteenth, in the [[concepts/hope|hope]] of

finding an entrance.



January 14.—This morning we reached the western extremity of the

field which had impeded us, and, weathering it, came to an open

sea, without a particle of ice. Upon sounding with two hundred

fathoms, we here found a current setting southwardly at the rate

of half a mile per hour. The temperature of the air was

forty-seven, that of the [[motifs/water|water]] thirty-four. We now sailed to the

southward without meeting any interruption of moment until the

sixteenth, when, at [[motifs/noon|noon]], we were in latitude 81 degrees 21’,

longitude 42 degrees W. We here again sounded, and found a

current setting still southwardly, and at the rate of three

quarters of a mile per hour. The variation per azimuth had

diminished, and the temperature of the air was mild and pleasant,

CAPITOLO 17





Titolo:  
Abbiamo proseguito verso sud per quattro giorni dopo aver abbandonato…

Cercare le isole di Glass, senza incontrare affatto alcun ghiaccio.

Il ventiseiesimo giorno, alle [[motifs/noon|mezzogiorno]], ci trovavamo a una latitudine di 63 gradi e 23 minuti.

S., longitudine 41 gradi 25’ O.: ora vedevamo diversi grandi blocchi di ghiaccio

Isole e un campo di ghiaccio… ma non certo di grandi dimensioni

Estensione. I venti soffiavano generalmente da sud-est.

A nord-est, ma erano molto leggere. Ogni volta che soffiava un vento occidentale,

Qualcosa che accadeva raramente, ma ogni volta era accompagnato inevitabilmente da un temporale improvviso.

Ogni giorno nevicava sempre di più. Il termometro, sulla.

Il ventisettesimo si trovava a trentacinque.



1 gennaio 1828 – In questo giorno ci trovammo completamente intrappolati.

Sotto il ghiaccio… e le nostre prospettive sembravano davvero poco promettenti. Una situazione difficile…

Un vento forte soffiò per tutto il pomeriggio da nord-est…

"Carri grandi pezzi di ghiaccio contro il timone e il controrullante..."

Con tale violenza che tutti noi tremavamo per le conseguenze.

Verso sera, la tempesta soffiava ancora con violenza; un vasto campo…

Titolo:  
“Separati in prima fila… e così fummo messi in condizione di procedere, semplicemente premendo un pulsante…”

"Navigare tra i frammenti più piccoli per trovare un passaggio verso lo spazio aperto."

Acqua oltre. Mentre ci avvicinavamo a quell’area, abbiamo levato le vele.

Degradi e distanze… alla fine, tutto si è chiarito, sotto un unico obiettivo comune.

Ammainò la vela di prua.



2 gennaio – Ora il tempo era abbastanza piacevole. A [[motifs/noon|mattina]] noi.

Ci trovavamo a una latitudine di 69 gradi e 10 minuti sud, e a una longitudine di 42…

20 gradi ovest: oltre il circolo antartico. Molto poco.

A sud si potevano vedere dei banchi di ghiaccio, anche se ne estendevano vaste aree.

Ormai è tutto alle nostre spalle. Oggi abbiamo montato alcuni attrezzi per le rilevazioni sonore, utilizzando…

Grande pentola di ferro in grado di contenere venti galloni, e una serie di…

Duecento braccia… Abbiamo individuato la corrente che scorre verso nord.

Circa un quarto di miglio all’ora… La temperatura dell’aria.

Ora aveva circa trentatré anni. Qui abbiamo riscontrato una variazione di 14.

28 gradi a est, in termini di azimut.



5 gennaio – Continuavamo ancora a dirigerci verso sud, senza alcun cambiamento significativo nelle nostre intenzioni…

Gravi ostacoli… Questa mattina, tuttavia, trovandosi a una latitudine di 73…

37 gradi 15’ est, 42 gradi 10’ ovest: ci trovavamo di nuovo lì

In piedi accanto a un immenso spazio di ghiaccio solido… Vedemmo…

Tuttavia, c'era molto [[motifs/water|acqua aperta]] a sud, e non provavo alcun [[concepts/doubt|dubbio]].

Raggiungerlo alla fine… In posizione verso est

Lungo il bordo dei blocchi di ghiaccio, alla fine arrivammo in un tratto…

Titolo:  
Dai circa un miglio di larghezza… attraverso cui ci siamo fatti strada.

Al tramonto… Il mare in cui ci trovavamo era coperto densamente da…

“Isole di ghiaccio, ma senza ghiaccio sul terreno; abbiamo proseguito con coraggio…”

Prima. Il freddo non sembrava aumentare, anche se c’era stata la [[motifs/snow|neve]].

Molto spesso, e di tanto in tanto, si verificano raffiche di grandine particolarmente violente.

Numerose stormi di albatros volarono sopra la goletta in quel giorno.

Da sud-est a nord-ovest.



7 gennaio. — Il mare era ancora abbastanza aperto, quindi noi.

Non ebbe alcuna difficoltà nel mantenere la nostra rotta. Verso ovest…

Ho visto alcuni iceberg di dimensioni incredibili, e nel pomeriggio sono passato oltre…

Molto vicino a qualcuno il cui apice doveva essere sicuramente alto almeno quattro…

“Cento braccia sotto la superficie dell’oceano… Il suo diametro era…”

Probabilmente, alla base, tre quarti di lega… e qualcos’altro ancora.

Fiumi di [[motifs/water|acqua]] scorrevano dalle fessure sui suoi fianchi. Noi.

Restò visibile da quest’isola per due giorni, e poi finalmente scomparve.

In una nebbia.



10 gennaio – All’alba di questa mattina abbiamo avuto la sfortuna di perdere…

“Uomo in mare… Si chiamava Peter Vredenburgh ed era americano.”

Nativo di [[settings/new-york|New York]], fu uno dei giocatori più preziosi della squadra.

Salire sulla scuola… Mentre si avvicinava alla prua, gli scivolò il piede.

Cadde tra due blocchi di ghiaccio e non si rialzò mai più. Alle [[motifs/noon|mattine]] di.

In quel giorno ci trovavamo a 78 gradi e 30 minuti di latitudine, 40 gradi di longitudine

15’ Ovest: Il freddo era ormai eccessivo, e ci furono raffiche di grandine

Continuamente da nord e da est… In questa direzione.

Ancora numerosi iceberg imponenti… e l’intero orizzonte

A est sembrava essere bloccato da ghiaccio, che si estendeva verso l’alto.

Disposti in strati, uno sopra l’altro; alcuni tronchi galleggianti passavano accanto.

Durante la sera, un gran numero di [[motifs/birds|uccelli]] volò sopra.

Tra cui c’erano nelli, petrelli, albatros e un grande uccello.

Titolo:  
Di un piumaggio di un blu brillante… La variazione in questo caso, in base all’azimut, era…

Meno di quanto fosse stato in precedenza prima del nostro passaggio attraverso l’Antartide

Circolo.



12 gennaio – Il nostro passaggio verso sud sembrava di nuovo improbabile…

Nella direzione del polo non si vedeva nulla se non una cosa…

Apparentemente illimitata, quella massa di materia era sostenuta da enormi [[settings/mountains|montagne]] di detriti frastagliati.

Ghiaccio… un precipizio dopo l’altro, tutti sollevati minacciosamente uno sopra l’altro. Noi…

Si trovava rivolto verso ovest fino al quattordicesimo giorno, nella speranza che.

Trovando un modo per entrare.



14 gennaio – Questa mattina abbiamo raggiunto l’estremità occidentale…

"Campo che ci aveva ostacolato… superandolo, arrivammo in un luogo aperto."

Mare senza una particella di ghiaccio. Al suono di duecento…

"Qui abbiamo riscontrato una corrente che si dirige verso sud a una certa velocità..."

Titolo:  
A mezzo miglio all’ora… La temperatura dell’aria era…

Quarantasette, quello dell’[[motifs/water|acqua]] trentaquattro. Ora abbiamo navigato verso.

Verso sud, senza incontrare alcuna interruzione per tutto il cammino…

Sedicesimo giorno: alle [[motifs/noon|mattine]], ci trovavamo a una latitudine di 81 gradi e 21 minuti.

Lungitudine 42 gradi Ovest. Siamo di nuovo qui e abbiamo trovato…

Titolo:  
La direzione attuale è ancora verso sud, e a un ritmo di tre…

Quarti di miglio all’ora… La variazione in base all’azimut…

La temperatura dell’aria era mite e piacevole.



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_17--part_02" data-title="The Narrative of A. Gordon Pym (Raven Edition) — Chapter 17 (part 2)" data-chapter="Chapter 17" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="archetype/monster,motif/animals,motif/birds,motif/blood,motif/secrets,motif/water,motif/well,concept/body,concept/honour,character/bottom"></span>


the thermometer being as high as fifty-one. At this period not a

particle of ice was to be discovered. All hands on board now felt

certain of attaining the pole.



January 17.—This day was full of incident. Innumerable flights of

[[motifs/birds|birds]] flew over us from the southward, and several were shot from

the deck, one of them, a species of pelican, proved to be

excellent eating. About midday a small floe of ice was seen from

the masthead off the larboard bow, and upon it there appeared to

be some large animal. As the weather was good and nearly calm,

Captain Guy ordered out two of the boats to see what it was. Dirk

Peters and myself accompanied the mate in the larger boat. Upon

coming up with the floe, we perceived that it was in the

possession of a gigantic creature of the race of the Arctic bear,

but far exceeding in size the largest of these [[motifs/animals|animals]]. Being

[[motifs/well|well]] armed, we made no scruple of attacking it at once. Several

shots were fired in quick succession, the most of which took

effect, apparently, in the head and [[concepts/body|body]]. Nothing discouraged,

however, the [[archetypes/monster|monster]] threw himself from the ice, and swam with

open jaws, to the boat in which were Peters and myself. Owing to

the confusion which ensued among us at this unexpected turn of

the adventure, no person was ready immediately with a second

shot, and the bear had actually succeeded in getting half his

vast bulk across our gunwale, and seizing one of the men by the

small of his back, before any efficient means were taken to repel

him. In this extremity nothing but the promptness and agility of

Peters saved us from destruction. Leaping upon the back of the

huge beast, he plunged the blade of a knife behind the neck,

reaching the spinal marrow at a blow. The brute tumbled into the

sea lifeless, and without a struggle, [[rolling]] over Peters as he

fell. The latter soon recovered himself, and a rope being thrown

him, he secured the carcass before entering the boat. We then

returned in triumph to the schooner, towing our trophy behind us.

This bear, upon admeasurement, proved to be full fifteen feet in

his greatest length. His wool was perfectly white, and very

coarse, curling tightly. The eyes were of a [[motifs/blood|blood]] red, and larger

than those of the Arctic bear, the snout also more rounded,

rather resembling the snout of the bulldog. The meat was tender,

but excessively rank and fishy, although the men devoured it with

avidity, and declared it excellent eating.



Scarcely had we got our prize alongside, when the man at the

masthead gave the joyful shout of “land on the starboard bow!”

All hands were now upon the alert, and, a breeze springing up

very opportunely from the northward and eastward, we were soon

close in with the coast. It proved to be a low rocky islet, of

about a league in circumference, and altogether destitute of

vegetation, if we except a species of prickly pear. In

approaching it from the northward, a singular ledge of rock is

seen projecting into the sea, and bearing a strong resemblance to

corded bales of cotton. Around this ledge to the westward is a

small bay, at the [[characters/bottom|bottom]] of which our boats effected a convenient

landing.



It did not take us long to explore every portion of the island,

but, with one exception, we found nothing worthy of our

observation. In the southern extremity, we picked up near the

shore, half buried in a pile of loose stones, a piece of wood,

which seemed to have formed the prow of a canoe. There had been

evidently some attempt at carving upon it, and Captain Guy

fancied that he made out the figure of a tortoise, but the

resemblance did not strike me very forcibly. Besides this prow,

if such it were, we found no other token that any living creature

had ever been here before. Around the coast we discovered

occasional small floes of ice—but these were very few. The exact

situation of the islet (to which Captain Guy gave the name of

Bennet’s Islet, in [[concepts/honour|honour]] of his partner in the ownership of the

schooner) is 82 degrees 50’ S. latitude, 42 degrees 20’ W.

longitude.



We had now advanced to the southward more than eight degrees

farther than any previous navigators, and the sea still lay

perfectly open before us. We found, too, that the variation

uniformly decreased as we proceeded, and, what was still more

surprising, that the temperature of the air, and latterly of the

[[motifs/water|water]], became milder. The weather might even be called pleasant,

and we had a steady but very gentle breeze always from some

northern point of the compass. The sky was usually clear, with

now and then a slight appearance of thin vapour in the southern

horizon—this, however, was invariably of brief duration. Two

difficulties [[Alone|alone]] presented themselves to our view; we were

getting short of fuel, and symptoms of scurvy had occurred among

several of the crew. These considerations began to impress upon

Captain Guy the necessity of returning, and he spoke of it

frequently. For my own part, confident as I was of soon arriving

at land of some description upon the course we were pursuing, and

having every reason to believe, from present appearances, that we

should not find it the sterile soil met with in the higher Arctic

latitudes, I warmly pressed upon him the expediency of

persevering, at least for a few days longer, in the direction we

were now holding. So tempting an opportunity of solving the great

problem in regard to an Antarctic continent had never yet been

afforded to man, and I confess that I felt myself bursting with

indignation at the timid and ill-timed suggestions of our

commander. I believe, indeed, that what I could not refrain from

saying to him on this head had the effect of inducing him to push

on. While, therefore, I cannot but lament the most unfortunate

and bloody events which immediately arose from my advice, I must

still be allowed to feel some degree of gratification at having

been instrumental, however remotely, in opening to the eye of

science one of the most intensely exciting [[motifs/secrets|secrets]] which has ever

engrossed its attention.

<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_18--part_01" data-title="The Narrative of A. Gordon Pym (Raven Edition) — Chapter 18 (part 1)" data-chapter="Chapter 18" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="motif/time,motif/water,motif/well,motif/wind,concept/body,character/bottom"></span>


CHAPTER 18





January 18.—This morning {*4} we continued to the southward, with

the same pleasant weather as before. The sea was entirely smooth,

the air tolerably warm and from the northeast, the temperature of

the [[motifs/water|water]] fifty-three. We now again got our sounding-gear in

order, and, with a hundred and fifty fathoms of line, found the

current setting toward the pole at the rate of a mile an hour.

This constant tendency to the southward, both in the [[motifs/wind|wind]] and

current, caused some degree of speculation, and even of alarm, in

different quarters of the schooner, and I saw distinctly that no

little impression had been made upon the mind of Captain Guy. He

was exceedingly sensitive to ridicule, however, and I finally

succeeded in laughing him out of his apprehensions. The variation

was now very trivial. In the course of the day we saw several

large whales of the right species, and innumerable flights of the

albatross passed over the vessel. We also picked up a bush, full

of red berries, like those of the hawthorn, and the carcass of a

singular-looking land-animal. It was three feet in length, and

but six inches in height, with four very short legs, the feet

armed with long claws of a brilliant scarlet, and resembling

coral in substance. The [[concepts/body|body]] was covered with a straight silky

hair, perfectly white. The tail was peaked like that of a rat,

and about a foot and a half long. The head resembled a cat’s,

with the exception of the ears—these were flopped like the ears

of a dog. The teeth were of the same brilliant scarlet as the

claws.



January 19.—To-day, being in latitude 83 degrees 20’, longitude

43 degrees 5’ W. (the sea being of an extraordinarily dark

colour), we again saw land from the masthead, and, upon a closer

scrutiny, found it to be one of a group of very large islands.

The shore was precipitous, and the interior seemed to be [[motifs/well|well]]

wooded, a circumstance which occasioned us great joy. In about

four hours from our first discovering the land we came to anchor

in ten fathoms, sandy [[characters/bottom|bottom]], a league from the coast, as a high

surf, with strong ripples here and there, rendered a nearer

approach of doubtful expediency. The two largest boats were now

ordered out, and a party, [[motifs/well|well]] armed (among whom were Peters and

myself), proceeded to look for an opening in the reef which

appeared to encircle the island. After searching about for some

[[motifs/time|time]], we discovered an inlet, which we were entering, when we saw

four large canoes put off from the shore, filled with men who

seemed to be [[motifs/well|well]] armed. We waited for them to come up, and, as

they moved with great rapidity, they were soon within hail.

Captain Guy now held up a white handkerchief on the blade of an

oar, when the strangers made a full stop, and commenced a loud

jabbering all at once, intermingled with occasional shouts, in

which we could distinguish the words Anamoo-moo! and Lama-Lama!

They continued this for at least half an hour, during which we

had a good opportunity of observing their appearance.



In the four canoes, which might have been fifty feet long and

five broad, there were a hundred and ten savages in all. They

were about the ordinary stature of Europeans, but of a more

muscular and brawny frame. Their complexion a jet black, with

thick and long woolly hair. They were clothed in skins of an

unknown black animal, shaggy and silky, and made to fit the [[concepts/body|body]]

with some degree of skill, the hair being inside, except where

turned out about the neck, wrists, and ankles. Their arms

consisted principally of clubs, of a dark, and apparently very

heavy wood. Some spears, however, were observed among them,

headed with flint, and a few slings. The bottoms of the canoes

were full of black stones about the size of a large egg.



When they had concluded their harangue (for it was clear they

intended their jabbering for such), one of them who seemed to be

the chief stood up in the prow of his canoe, and made signs for

us to bring our boats alongside of him. This hint we pretended

not to understand, thinking it the wiser plan to maintain, if

possible, the interval between us, as their number more than

quadrupled our own. Finding this to be the case, the chief

ordered the three other canoes to hold back, while he advanced

toward us with his own. As soon as he came up with us he leaped

on board the largest of our boats, and seated himself by the side

of Captain Guy, pointing at the same [[motifs/time|time]] to the schooner, and

repeating the word Anamoo-moo! and Lama-Lama! We now put back to

the vessel, the four canoes following at a little distance.



Upon getting alongside, the chief evinced symptoms of extreme

surprise and delight, clapping his hands, slapping his thighs and

breast, and laughing obstreperously. His followers behind joined

in his merriment, and for some minutes the din was so excessive

as to be absolutely deafening. Quiet being at length restored,

Captain Guy ordered the boats to be hoisted up, as a necessary

precaution, and gave the chief (whose name we soon found to be

Too-wit) to understand that we could admit no more than twenty of

his men on deck at one [[motifs/time|time]]. With this arrangement he appeared

perfectly satisfied, and gave some directions to the canoes, when

one of them approached, the rest remaining about fifty yards off.

Twenty of the savages now got on board, and proceeded to ramble

Sembrava essere ben armato. Aspettammo che si avvicinassero, e.

Parlando tutti insieme, a volte mescolando grida, in…

In questo modo riuscimmo a distinguere le parole “Anamoo-moo!” e “Lama-Lama!”.

Nelle quattro canoe, che potevano avere una lunghezza di cinquanta piedi…

Cinque gruppi, in totale centoventi selvaggi…

Titolo:  
Avevano una statura simile a quella degli europei comuni, ma…

Corpo muscoloso e robusto. La loro pelle è di un nero intenso…

Quando ebbero concluso il loro discorso appassionato…

Il capo si alzò nella prua della sua canoa e fece dei segni…

del Capitano Guy, che nello stesso [[motifs/time|momento]] indicò anche la goletta.

Sorpresa e gioia: batte le mani, si dà delle pacche sulle cosce…

Il silenzio, finalmente ripristinato…

“Precauzione… e il capo (il cui nome scoprimmo presto essere…”

<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_18--part_02" data-title="The Narrative of A. Gordon Pym (Raven Edition) — Chapter 18 (part 2)" data-chapter="Chapter 18" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="motif/home,motif/silence,motif/time,motif/water,motif/well,motif/wind,motif/winter,concept/hope,concept/self,concept/wonder,character/bottom"></span>


over every part of the deck, and scramble about among the

rigging, making themselves much at [[motifs/home|home]], and examining every

article with great inquisitiveness.



It was quite evident that they had never before seen any of the

white race—from whose complexion, indeed, they appeared to

recoil. They believed the Jane to be a living creature, and

seemed to be afraid of hurting it with the points of their

spears, carefully turning them up. Our crew were much amused with

the conduct of Too-wit in one instance. The cook was splitting

some wood near the galley, and, by accident, struck his axe into

the deck, making a gash of considerable depth. The chief

immediately ran up, and pushing the cook on one side rather

roughly, commenced a half whine, half howl, strongly indicative

of sympathy in what he considered the sufferings of the schooner,

patting and smoothing the gash with his hand, and washing it from

a bucket of seawater which stood by. This was a degree of

ignorance for which we were not prepared, and for my part I could

not help thinking some of it affected.



When the visitors had satisfied, as [[motifs/well|well]] as they could, their

curiosity in regard to our upper works, they were admitted below,

when their amazement exceeded all bounds. Their astonishment now

appeared to be far too deep for words, for they roamed about in

[[motifs/silence|silence]], broken only by low ejaculations. The arms afforded them

much food for speculation, and they were suffered to handle and

examine them at leisure. I do not believe that they had the least

suspicion of their actual use, but rather took them for idols,

seeing the care we had of them, and the attention with which we

watched their movements while handling them. At the great guns

their [[concepts/wonder|wonder]] was redoubled. They approached them with every mark

of the profoundest reverence and awe, but forbore to examine them

minutely. There were two large mirrors in the cabin, and here was

the acme of their amazement. Too-wit was the first to approach

them, and he had got in the middle of the cabin, with his face to

one and his back to the other, before he fairly perceived them.

Upon raising his eyes and seeing his reflected [[concepts/self|self]] in the glass,

I thought the savage would go mad; but, upon turning short round

to make a retreat, and beholding himself a second [[motifs/time|time]] in the

opposite direction, I was afraid he would expire upon the spot.

No [[Persuasion|persuasion]] could prevail upon him to take another look;

throwing himself upon the floor, with his face buried in his

hands, he remained thus until we were obliged to drag him upon

deck.



The whole of the savages were admitted on board in this manner,

twenty at a [[motifs/time|time]], Too-wit being suffered to remain during the

entire period. We saw no disposition to thievery among them, nor

did we miss a single article after their departure. Throughout

the whole of their visit they evinced the most friendly manner.

There were, however, some points in their demeanour which we

found it impossible to understand; for example, we could not get

them to approach several very harmless objects—such as the

schooner’s sails, an egg, an open book, or a pan of flour. We

endeavoured to ascertain if they had among them any articles

which might be turned to account in the way of traffic, but found

great difficulty in being comprehended. We made out,

nevertheless, what greatly astonished us, that the islands

abounded in the large tortoise of the Gallipagos, one of which we

saw in the canoe of Too-wit. We saw also some biche de mer in the

hands of one of the savages, who was greedily devouring it in its

natural state. These anomalies—for they were such when considered

in regard to the latitude—induced Captain Guy to wish for a

thorough investigation of the country, in the [[concepts/hope|hope]] of making a

profitable speculation in his discovery. For my own part, anxious

as I was to know something more of these islands, I was still

more earnestly bent on prosecuting the voyage to the southward

without delay. We had now fine weather, but there was no telling

how long it would last; and being already in the eighty-fourth

parallel, with an open sea before us, a current setting strongly

to the southward, and the [[motifs/wind|wind]] fair, I could not listen with any

patience to a proposition of stopping longer than was absolutely

necessary for the health of the crew and the taking on board a

proper supply of fuel and fresh provisions. I represented to the

captain that we might easily make this group on our return, and

[[motifs/winter|winter]] here in the event of being blocked up by the ice. He at

length came into my views (for in some way, hardly known to

myself, I had acquired much influence over him), and it was

finally resolved that, even in the event of our finding biche de

mer, we should only stay here a week to recruit, and then push on

to the southward while we might. Accordingly we made every

necessary preparation, and, under the guidance of Too-wit, got

the Jane through the reef in safety, coming to anchor about a

mile from the shore, in an excellent bay, completely landlocked,

on the southeastern coast of the main island, and in ten fathoms

of [[motifs/water|water]], black sandy [[characters/bottom|bottom]]. At the head of this bay there were

three fine springs (we were told) of good [[motifs/water|water]], and we saw

abundance of wood in the vicinity. The four canoes followed us


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

Dappertutto sul ponte, e si muovono in giro tra…

Installando delle attrezzature, si sentivano molto a proprio agio in quel luogo e esaminavano ogni dettaglio.

Un articolo scritto con grande curiosità.



Era evidente che non avessero mai visto nulla del genere prima d’allora

Razza bianca: dal cui colore della pelle, infatti, sembravano derivare le loro caratteristiche

Ritirarsi inorriditi. Credevano che la “Jane” fosse una creatura vivente…

Sembrava temessero di danneggiarlo con le loro punte…

“Speari, che venivano girati con cura… Il nostro equipaggio ne fu molto divertito.”

Il comportamento di Too-wit in un certo momento… Il cuoco stava tagliando qualcosa.

Un pezzo di legno vicino alla galera… e, per caso, la sua ascia lo colpì

Il ponte, squarciato da una ferita profonda… Il capo

Corse immediatamente verso di lui e, spingendo da parte il cuoco…

Un lamento a metà grido, a metà ululato, decisamente significativo…

Di compassione per ciò che considerava le sofferenze della goletta

"#Accarezzando e lisciando la ferita con la mano, la pulì..."

“Un secchio d’acqua di mare che era lì pronto… Questo rappresentava un certo livello…”

Ignoranza di fronte alla quale non eravamo preparati… e per quanto mi riguarda, io potevo solo…

Non posso fare a meno di pensare che alcune di queste cose abbiano avuto un impatto.



Quando i visitatori ebbero soddisfatto, nel miglior modo possibile, le loro.

Curiosità riguardo alle nostre opere superiori… furono ammesse al di sotto.

Quando la loro meraviglia superò ogni limite… La loro sorpresa, ora…

Sembrava un argomento troppo profondo per essere espresso a parole… quelle parole, infatti, vagavano senza una direzione precisa.

Il [[motifs/silence|silenzio]], interrotto solo da deboli gemiti. Le braccia li avvolgevano protettivamente.

Molto materiale per speculazioni… e vennero lasciati liberi di occuparsene.

“Esaminerli con calma… Non credo che avessero la minima…”

Sospetto riguardo al loro vero uso: li consideravano piuttosto degli idoli.

"#Vedendo la cura che abbiamo avuto per loro e l’attenzione con cui li abbiamo trattati..."

Li osservavo mentre li maneggiavano… Quei grandi cannoni.

La loro [[concepts/wonder|meraviglia]] aumentò ancora di più. Si avvicinarono a loro con ogni possibile precauzione.

Con la più profonda reverenza e timore, ma senza osare esaminarle.

“Minuziosamente… C’erano due grandi specchi nella cabina…”

Il culmine della loro meraviglia… Too-wit fu il primo ad avvicinarsi.

Loro, e si era trovato nel mezzo della cabina, con il viso rivolto…

Uno dietro l'altro, prima che riuscisse a vederli chiaramente.

Alzando lo sguardo e vedendo il proprio riflesso nello specchio,

Pensavo che quel selvaggio impazzisse… ma invece si è girato di scatto.

Per fare ritirata, si rese conto di trovarsi per la seconda volta in quella situazione.

In direzione opposta, temevo che potesse morire sul colpo.

Nessuna [[Persuasion|persuasione]] riuscì a convincerlo a dare un'altra occhiata.

Gettandosi a terra, con il viso sepolto nel…

Mani… rimase così fino a quando non fummo costretti a trascinarlo via con noi.

Mazzo.



Tutti i selvaggi furono fatti salire a bordo in questo modo.

Venti persone contemporaneamente; Too-wit fu costretto ad attendere durante tutto quel tempo.

Intero periodo: non osservammo alcuna tendenza al furto tra di loro, né…

Abbiamo perso qualche articolo dopo la loro partenza? Nel corso del tempo…

Durante l’intera durata della loro visita, dimostrarono il comportamento più amichevole possibile.

C'erano tuttavia alcuni aspetti del loro comportamento che…

Non riuscimmo assolutamente a comprenderlo; ad esempio, non fummo in grado di capirne il significato.

"Farli avvicinare a diversi oggetti del tutto inoffensivi… come ad esempio…"

“Le vele della goletta, un uovo, un libro aperto… o una ciotola di farina.”

Si è cercato di verificare se tra loro ci fossero alcuni articoli.

Titolo:  
Qualcosa che potrebbe essere utilizzato per migliorare il traffico, ma…

Grande difficoltà nel essere compresi… Ci siamo capiti lo stesso.

Tuttavia, ciò che ci sorprese maggiormente fu… quelle isole

Nelle grandi tartarughe delle Galapagos ce n’era in abbondanza; una di queste…

Nella canoa di Too-wit… Vedemmo anche alcune “biche de mer”.

Mani di uno dei selvaggi che lo stava divorando con avidità

Stato naturale… Queste anomalie: perché lo erano, quando venivano considerate in quel modo.

In merito alla latitudine… il Capitano Guy desiderò qualcosa.

Indagine approfondita del paese, nella [[concepts/hope|speranza]] di poter fare qualcosa.

Speculazioni proficue sulla sua scoperta… Per quanto mi riguarda, sono ansioso.

Come avrei poi scoperto, riguardo a queste isole…

Con maggiore determinazione deciso a proseguire il viaggio verso sud

Senza indugio. Ora il tempo era bello, ma non si poteva mai sapere…

Titolo:  
Per quanto tempo potrebbe durare… e essendo già arrivato all’ottantatreesimo…

Titolo:  
In parallelo… con un mare aperto davanti a noi, un contesto che si sviluppa con forza…

Verso sud, e con il vento che soffiava dolcemente, non riuscivo proprio a prestare attenzione a nulla.

Pazienza di fronte a una proposta che richiede un tempo di attesa superiore al necessario

Necessario per la salute dell’equipaggio e per l’imbarco di…

Approvvigionamento adeguato di carburante e provviste fresche. Ho rappresentato questo punto alle autorità competenti.

Capitano, potremmo facilmente riunire questo gruppo al nostro ritorno…

[[motifs/winter|Inverno]], qui, nel caso venisse bloccato dal ghiaccio. Lui.

“La lunghezza entrò nel mio campo visivo… (perché, in qualche modo, quasi sconosciuto…”

"#Io stesso avevo acquisito su di lui una notevole influenza...", e fu così."

Finalmente deciso che, anche nel caso in cui trovassimo…

Titolo:  
Dovremmo rimanere qui solo una settimana per reclutare le persone necessarie, e poi proseguire il nostro cammino.

Verso sud, finché ne avevamo la possibilità. E così facemmo.

Titolo:  
La necessaria preparazione, e sotto la guida di Too-wit, fu completata.

La Jane attraversa il banco di scogli senza problemi, gettando l’ancora poco dopo…

A un miglio dalla riva, in una baia incantevole, completamente isolata dalla terraferma…

Sulla costa sud-orientale dell’isola principale, e a una profondità di dieci braccia…

Acqua[[motifs/water|,]], fondo sabbioso e nero[[characters/bottom|,]]. All’estremità di questa baia si trovavano.

Tre sorgenti limpide, ci fu detto, con acqua di ottima qualità; le abbiamo viste con i nostri occhi.

Abbondanza di legna nelle vicinanze… I quattro canoë ci seguirono.



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_18--part_03" data-title="The Narrative of A. Gordon Pym (Raven Edition) — Chapter 18 (part 3)" data-chapter="Chapter 18" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="motif/mirror,motif/nature,motif/time,motif/water,motif/well,concept/nature,form/novel"></span>


in, keeping, however, at a respectful distance. Too-wit himself

remained on board, and, upon our dropping anchor, invited us to

accompany him on shore, and visit his village in the interior. To

this Captain Guy consented; and ten savages being left on board

as hostages, a party of us, twelve in all, got in readiness to

attend the chief. We took care to be [[motifs/well|well]] armed, yet without

evincing any distrust. The schooner had her guns run out, her

boarding-nettings up, and every other proper precaution was taken

to guard against surprise. Directions were left with the chief

mate to admit no person on board during our absence, and, in the

event of our not appearing in twelve hours, to send the cutter,

with a swivel, around the island in search of us.



At every step we took inland the conviction forced itself upon us

that we were in a country differing essentially from any hitherto

visited by civilized men. We saw nothing with which we had been

formerly conversant. The trees resembled no growth of either the

torrid, the temperate, or the northern frigid zones, and were

altogether unlike those of the lower southern latitudes we had

already traversed. The very rocks were [[forms/novel|novel]] in their mass, their

color, and their stratification; and the streams themselves,

utterly incredible as it may appear, had so little in common with

those of other climates, that we were scrupulous of tasting them,

and, indeed, had difficulty in bringing ourselves to believe that

their qualities were purely those of [[concepts/nature|nature]]. At a small brook

which crossed our path (the first we had reached) Too-wit and his

attendants halted to drink. On account of the singular character

of the [[motifs/water|water]], we refused to taste it, supposing it to be

polluted; and it was not until some [[motifs/time|time]] afterward we came to

understand that such was the appearance of the streams throughout

the whole group. I am at a loss to give a distinct idea of the

[[concepts/nature|nature]] of this liquid, and cannot do so without many words.

Although it flowed with rapidity in all declivities where common

[[motifs/water|water]] would do so, yet never, except when falling in a cascade,

had it the customary appearance of limpidity. It was,

nevertheless, in point of fact, as perfectly limpid as any

limestone [[motifs/water|water]] in existence, the difference being only in

appearance. At first sight, and especially in cases where little

declivity was found, it bore resemblance, as regards consistency,

to a thick infusion of gum arabic in common [[motifs/water|water]]. But this was

only the least remarkable of its extraordinary qualities. It was

not colourless, nor was it of any one uniform colour—presenting

to the eye, as it flowed, every possible shade of purple; like

the hues of a changeable silk. This variation in shade was

produced in a manner which excited as profound astonishment in

the minds of our party as the [[motifs/mirror|mirror]] had done in the case of

Too-wit. Upon collecting a basinful, and allowing it to settle

thoroughly, we perceived that the whole mass of liquid was made

up of a number of distinct veins, each of a distinct hue; that

these veins did not commingle; and that their cohesion was

perfect in regard to their own particles among themselves, and

imperfect in regard to neighbouring veins. Upon passing the blade

of a knife athwart the veins, the [[motifs/water|water]] closed over it

immediately, as with us, and also, in withdrawing it, all traces

of the passage of the knife were instantly obliterated. If,

however, the blade was passed down accurately between the two

veins, a perfect separation was effected, which the power of

cohesion did not immediately rectify. The phenomena of this [[motifs/water|water]]

formed the first definite link in that vast chain of apparent

miracles with which I was destined to be at length encircled.


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

A distanza rispettosa… anche se troppo vicino.

Rimase a bordo e, non appena gettammo l’ancora, ci invitò…

Accompagnarlo sulla terraferma e visitare il suo villaggio nell’entroterra.

Il capitano Guy acconsentì; e dieci selvaggi rimasero a bordo.

In qualità di ostaggi, un gruppo di noi, dodici in totale, ci preparammo…

Aspettiamo il capo. Ci siamo assicurati di essere ben armati, ma senza.

“Senza mostrare alcun segno di diffidenza… La goletta aveva esaurito le sue armi…”

“Le reti di protezione sono state installate, e tutte le altre misure preventive necessarie sono state adottate.”

Per prevenire eventuali sorprese: le istruzioni furono lasciate al capo.

"Non ammettere nessuno a bordo durante la nostra assenza, e..."

"In caso non ci presentassimo entro dodici ore, inviate il cutter..."

Con un meccanismo girevole, girava intorno all’isola alla nostra ricerca.



A ogni passo che facemmo verso l’interno, quella convinzione si impose su di noi.

Titolo:  
Che ci trovavamo in un paese sostanzialmente diverso da qualsiasi altro conosciuto fino ad allora…

Visitato da uomini civili… Non abbiamo visto nulla che potesse interessarci.

Un tempo familiare… Gli alberi non assomigliavano a nessuna forma di vegetazione conosciuta.

Zone torride, zone temperate o zone settentrionali fredde… e così via.

Del tutto diversi da quelli delle regioni a latitudini più basse del sud…

Già attraversato. Anche le rocce stesse erano [[forms/novel|nuove]] nella loro forma complessiva.

Colore e le loro stratificazioni; nonché i corsi d’acqua stessi

Titolo:  
Per quanto possa sembrare incredibile, aveva ben poco in comune con…

Titolo:  
Quelli di altre climatiche… che abbiamo evitato con scrupolo di assaggiare.

E, infatti, avevamo difficoltà ad credere davvero in ciò.

Le loro qualità erano puramente quelle della [[concepts/nature|natura]]. Presso un piccolo ruscello.

Quelli che ci hanno incrociato la strada… (i primi che abbiamo incontrato) Too-wit e i suoi compagni

Gli assistenti si fermarono per bere… A causa di quel carattere unico.

Dell’[[motifs/water|acqua]], rifiutammo di assaggiarla, pensando che fosse.

Inquinato. E fu solo dopo un po’ che riuscimmo a.

Si può intuire che tale fosse l’aspetto di quei corsi d’acqua in tutto il loro percorso.

Tutta il gruppo… Non so proprio come descriverlo in modo chiaro.

La [[concepts/nature|natura]] di questo liquido è tale che non si può descrivere senza utilizzare molte parole.

Nonostante scorresse con rapidità lungo tutte le pendenze comuni…

L’[[motifs/water|acqua]] potrebbe farlo, ma mai, tranne quando scorre a cascata.

Aveva l’aspetto consueto di chiarezza… Era proprio così.

Comunque sia, in realtà, altrettanto chiaro e limpido di qualsiasi altro

Acqua calcarea esistente; la differenza risiede soltanto nel.

Aspetto esteriore. A prima vista, soprattutto nei casi in cui ci sono pochi dettagli visibili…

Fu riscontrata una somiglianza, in termini di coerenza…

una densa infusione di gomma arabica in acqua comune. Ma questo era.

Solo la qualità meno straordinaria tra tutte le sue caratteristiche eccezionali… Era così.

Non era né incolore, né presentava un’unica tonalità uniforme: mostrava invece…

All'occhio, mentre scorreva, mostrava ogni possibile tonalità di viola; come…

“I colori di una seta mutevole: questa variazione di tonalità…”

Realizzato in un modo che suscitò profondo stupore…

Le menti del nostro partito, proprio come aveva fatto lo [[motifs/mirror|specchio]] nel caso di.

Troppo saputo… Dopo aver raccolto una coppa piena di liquido e averlo lasciato riposare…

Completamente, ci rendemmo conto che l’intera massa di liquido era composta…

Composto da diverse venature, ciascuna di un colore diverso; quel…

Queste vene non si mescolavano tra loro; e la loro coesione era…

Perfetti riguardo alle loro particelle interne, e…

Imperfetto rispetto alle vene adiacenti… Al passaggio della lama…

Con un coltello che attraversava le vene, l’[[motifs/water|acqua]] si chiuse sopra di esse.

Immediatamente, proprio come noi… e anche nel ritirarlo, tutte le tracce scompaiono.

Il passaggio del coltello venne immediatamente cancellato… Se.

Comunque, la lama fu tramandata con precisione tra i due.

Titolo:  
Vene: fu effettuata una separazione perfetta, grazie alla potenza…

La coesione non si ripristinò immediatamente; i fenomeni legati a questo [[motifs/water|acqua]].

Il primo anello concreto di quella vasta catena di eventi apparentemente casuali

Miracoli con i quali ero destinato, alla fine, ad essere circondato.



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_19--part_01" data-title="The Narrative of A. Gordon Pym (Raven Edition) — Chapter 19 (part 1)" data-chapter="Chapter 19" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="motif/animals,motif/birds,motif/home,motif/road,motif/water,concept/body,concept/faith"></span>


CHAPTER 19





We were nearly three hours in reaching the village, it being more

than nine miles in the interior, and the path lying through a

rugged country. As we passed along, the party of Too-wit (the

whole hundred and ten savages of the canoes) was momentarily

strengthened by smaller detachments, of from two to six or seven,

which joined us, as if by accident, at different turns of the

[[motifs/road|road]]. There appeared so much of system in this that I could not

help feeling distrust, and I spoke to Captain Guy of my

apprehensions. It was now too late, however, to recede, and we

concluded that our best security lay in evincing a perfect

confidence in the good [[concepts/faith|faith]] of Too-wit. We accordingly went on,

keeping a wary eye upon the manoeuvres of the savages, and not

permitting them to divide our numbers by pushing in between. In

this way, passing through a precipitous ravine, we at length

reached what we were told was the only collection of habitations

upon the island. As we came in sight of them, the chief set up a

shout, and frequently repeated the word Klock-klock, which we

supposed to be the name of the village, or perhaps the generic

name for villages.



The dwellings were of the most miserable description imaginable,

and, unlike those of even the lowest of the savage races with

which mankind are acquainted, were of no uniform plan. Some of

them (and these we found belonged to the Wampoos or Yampoos, the

great men of the land) consisted of a tree cut down at about four

feet from the root, with a large black skin thrown over it, and

hanging in loose folds upon the ground. Under this the savage

nestled. Others were formed by means of rough limbs of trees,

with the withered foliage upon them, made to recline, at an angle

of forty-five degrees, against a bank of clay, heaped up, without

regular form, to the height of five or six feet. Others, again,

were mere holes dug in the earth perpendicularly, and covered

over with similar branches, these being removed when the tenant

was about to enter, and pulled on again when he had entered. A

few were built among the forked limbs of trees as they stood, the

upper limbs being partially cut through, so as to bend over upon

the lower, thus forming thicker shelter from the weather. The

greater number, however, consisted of small shallow caverns,

apparently scratched in the face of a precipitous ledge of dark

stone, resembling fuller’s earth, with which three sides of the

village were bounded. At the door of each of these primitive

caverns was a small rock, which the tenant carefully placed

before the entrance upon leaving his residence, for what purpose

I could not ascertain, as the stone itself was never of

sufficient size to close up more than a third of the opening.



This village, if it were worthy of the name, lay in a valley of

some depth, and could only be approached from the southward, the

precipitous ledge of which I have already spoken cutting off all

access in other directions. Through the middle of the valley ran

a brawling stream of the same magical-looking [[motifs/water|water]] which has

been described. We saw several strange [[motifs/animals|animals]] about the

dwellings, all appearing to be thoroughly domesticated. The

largest of these creatures resembled our common hog in the

structure of the [[concepts/body|body]] and snout; the tail, however, was bushy,

and the legs slender as those of the antelope. Its motion was

exceedingly awkward and indecisive, and we never saw it attempt

to run. We noticed also several [[motifs/animals|animals]] very similar in

appearance, but of a greater length of [[concepts/body|body]], and covered with a

black wool. There were a great variety of tame fowls running

about, and these seemed to constitute the chief food of the

natives. To our astonishment we saw black albatross among these

[[motifs/birds|birds]] in a state of entire domestication, going to sea

periodically for food, but always returning to the village as a

[[motifs/home|home]], and using the southern shore in the vicinity as a place of

incubation. There they were joined by their friends the pelicans

as usual, but these latter never followed them to the dwellings

of the savages. Among the other kinds of tame fowls were ducks,

differing very little from the canvass-back of our own country,

black gannets, and a large bird not unlike the buzzard in

appearance, but not carnivorous. Of fish there seemed to be a

great abundance. We saw, during our visit, a quantity of dried

salmon, rock cod, blue dolphins, mackerel, blackfish, skate,

conger eels, elephantfish, mullets, soles, parrotfish,

leather-jackets, gurnards, hake, flounders, paracutas, and

innumerable other varieties. We noticed, too, that most of them

were similar to the fish about the group of Lord Auckland

Islands, in a latitude as low as fifty-one degrees south. The

Gallipago tortoise was also very plentiful. We saw but few wild

[[motifs/animals|animals]], and none of a large size, or of a species with which we

were familiar. One or two serpents of a formidable aspect crossed

our path, but the natives paid them little attention, and we

concluded that they were not venomous.



As we approached the village with Too-wit and his party, a vast

crowd of the people rushed out to meet us, with loud shouts,

among which we could only distinguish the everlasting Anamoo-moo!

and Lama-Lama! We were much surprised at perceiving that, with

one or two exceptions, these new comers were entirely naked, and


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

CAPITOLO 19





Ci vollero quasi tre ore per raggiungere il villaggio…

Più di nove miglia nell’entroterra, e il sentiero che attraversa…

Paese selvaggio e inospitale… Mentre procedevamo, il gruppo di Too-wit…

“Cento e dieci selvaggi delle canoe… per un momento…”

Rafforzati da piccoli distaccamenti composti da due a sei o sette unità.

Che ci ha raggiunti, come per caso, in momenti diversi…

[[motifs/road|strada]]. C'era così tanto di sistematico in tutto ciò che non riuscivo a.

Aiutare a superare il senso di sfiducia… Ho parlato con il Capitano Guy a riguardo.

Apprensioni… Ora, però, era troppo tardi per tornare indietro, e noi…

Si concluse che la nostra migliore forma di sicurezza risiedesse nel dimostrare di essere perfetti.

Fiducia nella buona [[concepts/faith|fede]] di Too-wit. Pertanto, proseguimmo il nostro cammino.

Tenendo d’occhio con attenzione le manovre di quei selvaggi… e non lasciandosi ingannare.

Facendoli infiltrare tra di noi, permettono loro di dividere le nostre forze.

Di qua, attraverso una ripida gola, alla fine…

Raggiunse quella che ci era stata descritta come l’unica collezione di abitazioni esistente.

Sull’isola. Non appena li avvistammo, il capo…

“Shout” e ripeteva spesso la parola “Klock-klock”.

Il presunto nome del villaggio… o forse qualcosa di più generico…

Nomi per i villaggi.



Le abitazioni erano delle peggiori condizioni che si possa immaginare.

E, a differenza di quelle delle razze selvagge più primitive…

I metodi conosciuti dall’umanità non seguivano un piano uniforme; alcuni di essi…

Loro (e questi che abbiamo trovato appartenevano ai Wampoos o ai Yampoos)

"Grandi uomini della terra": un albero tagliato all’altezza di circa quattro..."

"Tagliati alla radice, avvolti in una grande pelle nera..."

Distesi a mucchi sul terreno… Sotto di essi, la selvaggia natura…

Nascosti tra gli alberi… Altri erano realizzati utilizzando rami ruvidi e grezzi degli alberi stessi.

Con le foglie appassite ancora attaccate, erano state fatte inclinare in un certo angolo.

Di quarantacinque gradi, contro un banco di argilla accumulata, senza…

Forma regolare, alta circa cinque o sei piedi. Altri, invece…

Titolo:  
Sei semplicemente buchi scavati verticalmente nella terra e coperti…

Titolo:  
Con rami simili anch’essi rimossi quando l’inquilino…

Stava per entrare, ma si tirò indietro non appena lo fece.

Poche furono costruite tra i rami biforcati degli alberi, così com’erano.

Arti superiori parzialmente tagliati, al fine di poter piegarsi in avanti

La parte inferiore, quindi, forma un riparo più spesso contro il maltempo.

La maggior parte di queste cavità, tuttavia, era costituita da piccole e poco profonde grotte.

Chiaramente graffiato sul volto di una scarpata oscura e ripida

Titolo:  
Pietra simile alla terra di Fuller, con la quale sono stati rivestiti tre lati…

Il villaggio era delimitato da confini precisi. Alla porta di ogni abitazione di queste case primitive…

Titolo:  
Una piccola roccia nelle caverne… che l’inquilino posizionò con cura.

Prima di uscire dalla sua residenza, per quale motivo?

Non riuscii a stabilirlo, poiché la pietra stessa non era mai stata…

Dimensioni sufficienti per coprire più di un terzo dell’apertura.



Questo villaggio, se davvero meritasse tale nome, sorgeva in una valle…

Una profondità inaccessibile, raggiungibile solo da sud…

“La scogliera ripida di cui ho già parlato, che taglia completamente la strada…”

Accessi in altre direzioni… Lungo il centro della valle scorreva…

Un ruscello impetuoso di quella stessa acqua dal aspetto magico, che già possiede.

Sono stati descritti in questo modo. Abbiamo visto diversi strani [[motifs/animals|animali]] nelle vicinanze.

Abitazioni, tutte apparentemente completamente addomesticate.

Il più grande di questi esseri assomigliava al nostro comune maiale…

La struttura del [[concepts/body|corpo]] e del muso; la coda, invece, era folta.

E le gambe sottili come quelle di un’antilope… Il suo movimento era…

Estremamente impacciato e indeciso… e non lo vedemmo mai tentare nulla.

Per correre. Abbiamo notato anche diversi [[motifs/animals|animali]] molto simili tra loro.

Aspetto esteriore simile, ma con un corpo più lungo, e ricoperto di.

“Black Wool: Una grande varietà di pollame addomesticato correva in giro…”

Su questi, e sembrava che costituissero l’alimento principale…

Nativi… A nostra grande sorpresa, vedemmo tra di loro albatros neri.

[[motifs/birds|Uccelli]] completamente addomesticati, che vanno in mare.

Periodicamente si allontanava dal villaggio in cerca di cibo, ma tornava sempre indietro.

A [[motifs/home|casa]], utilizzando la riva meridionale delle vicinanze come luogo.

Incubazione. Lì furono raggiunti dai loro amici i pellicani.

Come al solito, ma queste ultime volte non li hanno mai seguiti fino alle abitazioni.

Dei selvaggi… Tra gli altri tipi di pollame addomesticato c’erano anche anatre.

Poco diverso dal paesaggio del nostro stesso Paese

Neri gabbiani e un grande uccello simile al gufo

Aspetto esteriore, ma non carnivoro… Tra i pesci, sembrava esserci uno…

Grande abbondanza. Durante la nostra visita, abbiamo visto una grande quantità di prodotti essiccati.

Salmone, merluzzo di roccia, delfini blu, sgombro, pesce nero, razza

Pesce coniglio, pesce elefante, sgombri, pesce sole, pesce pappagallo

Giubbotti di pelle, tute protettive, aringhe, merluzzi, paracaduti… e altro ancora.

Innumerevoli altre varietà… Abbiamo anche notato che la maggior parte di esse…

Titolo: Simili ai pesci intorno al gruppo di Lord Auckland

Isole, in una latitudine così bassa come cinquantuno gradi sud.

La tartaruga di Galipagos era anch’essa molto abbondante; ne abbiamo viste poche in natura.

[[motifs/animals|animali]], e nessuno di grandi dimensioni, né di una specie con cui noi.

Titolo:  
Erano familiari… Uno o due serpenti di aspetto minaccioso attraversarono il campo…

Il nostro cammino… ma i nativi prestavano loro poca attenzione, e noi…

Conclusero che non erano velenosi.



Mentre ci avvicinavamo al villaggio insieme a Too-wit e il suo gruppo, un vasto…

Una folla di persone ci accolse correndo fuori, gridando ad alta voce.

Tra queste, riuscivamo a distinguere soltanto l’eterno “Anamoo-moo”!

E il Lama-Lama! Siamo rimasti molto sorpresi nel constatare che…

A parte una o due eccezioni, questi nuovi arrivati erano completamente nudi.



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_19--part_02" data-title="The Narrative of A. Gordon Pym (Raven Edition) — Chapter 19 (part 2)" data-chapter="Chapter 19" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="motif/cross,motif/death,motif/leaves,motif/silence,motif/well,concept/beauty,concept/freedom,concept/friendship,character/bottom"></span>


skins being used only by the men of the canoes. All the weapons

of the country seemed also to be in the possession of the latter,

for there was no appearance of any among the villagers. There

were a great many women and children, the former not altogether

wanting in what might be termed personal [[concepts/beauty|beauty]]. They were

straight, tall, and [[motifs/well|well]] formed, with a grace and [[concepts/freedom|freedom]] of

carriage not to be found in civilized society. Their lips,

however, like those of the men, were thick and clumsy, so that,

even when laughing, the teeth were never disclosed. Their hair

was of a finer texture than that of the males. Among these naked

villagers there might have been ten or twelve who were clothed,

like the party of Too-wit, in dresses of black skin, and armed

with lances and heavy clubs. These appeared to have great

influence among the rest, and were always addressed by the title

Wampoo. These, too, were the tenants of the black skin palaces.

That of Too-wit was situated in the centre of the village, and

was much larger and somewhat better constructed than others of

its kind. The tree which formed its support was cut off at a

distance of twelve feet or thereabouts from the root, and there

were several branches left just below the cut, these serving to

extend the covering, and in this way prevent its flapping about

the trunk. The covering, too, which consisted of four very large

skins fastened together with wooden skewers, was secured at the

[[characters/bottom|bottom]] with pegs driven through it and into the ground. The floor

was strewed with a quantity of dry [[motifs/leaves|leaves]] by way of carpet.



To this hut we were conducted with great solemnity, and as many

of the natives crowded in after us as possible. Too-wit seated

himself on the [[motifs/leaves|leaves]], and made signs that we should follow his

example. This we did, and presently found ourselves in a

situation peculiarly uncomfortable, if not indeed critical. We

were on the ground, twelve in number, with the savages, as many

as forty, sitting on their hams so closely around us that, if any

disturbance had arisen, we should have found it impossible to

make use of our arms, or indeed to have risen to our feet. The

pressure was not only inside the tent, but outside, where

probably was every individual on the whole island, the crowd

being prevented from trampling us to [[motifs/death|death]] only by the incessant

exertions and vociferations of Too-wit. Our chief security lay,

however, in the presence of Too-wit himself among us, and we

resolved to stick by him closely, as the best chance of

extricating ourselves from the dilemma, sacrificing him

immediately upon the first appearance of hostile design.



After some trouble a certain degree of quiet was restored, when

the chief addressed us in a speech of great length, and very

nearly resembling the one delivered in the canoes, with the

exception that the Anamoo-moos! were now somewhat more

strenuously insisted upon than the Lama-Lamas! We listened in

profound [[motifs/silence|silence]] until the conclusion of this harangue, when

Captain Guy replied by assuring the chief of his eternal

[[concepts/friendship|friendship]] and goodwill, concluding what he had to say by a

present of several strings of blue beads and a knife. At the

former the monarch, much to our surprise, turned up his nose with

some expression of contempt, but the knife gave him the most

unlimited satisfaction, and he immediately ordered dinner. This

was handed into the tent over the heads of the attendants, and

consisted of the palpitating entrails of a specialis of unknown

animal, probably one of the slim-legged hogs which we had

observed in our approach to the village. Seeing us at a loss how

to proceed, he began, by way of setting us an example, to devour

yard after yard of the enticing food, until we could positively

stand it no longer, and evinced such manifest symptoms of

rebellion of stomach as inspired his majesty with a degree of

astonishment only inferior to that brought about by the

looking-glasses. We declined, however, partaking of the

delicacies before us, and endeavoured to make him understand that

we had no appetite whatever, having just finished a hearty

dejeuner.



When the monarch had made an end of his meal, we commenced a

series of [[motifs/cross|cross]]-questioning in every ingenious manner we could

devise, with a view of discovering what were the chief

productions of the country, and whether any of them might be

turned to profit. At length he seemed to have some idea of our

meaning, and offered to accompany us to a part of coast where he

assured us the biche de mer (pointing to a specimen of that

animal) was to be found in great abundance. We were glad of this

early opportunity of escaping from the oppression of the crowd,

and signified our eagerness to proceed. We now left the tent,

and, accompanied by the whole population of the village, followed

the chief to the southeastern extremity of the island, nor far

from the bay where our vessel lay at anchor. We waited here for

about an hour, until the four canoes were brought around by some

of the savages to our station. The whole of our party then

getting into one of them, we were paddled along the edge of the

reef before mentioned, and of another still farther out, where we

saw a far greater quantity of biche de mer than the oldest seamen

among us had ever seen in those groups of the lower latitudes

most celebrated for this article of commerce. We stayed near

these reefs only long enough to satisfy ourselves that we could

easily load a dozen vessels with the animal if necessary, when we

were taken alongside the schooner, and parted with Too-wit, after

obtaining from him a promise that he would bring us, in the

course of twenty-four hours, as many of the canvass-back ducks

and Gallipago tortoises as his canoes would hold. In the whole of

this adventure we saw nothing in the demeanour of the natives

calculated to create suspicion, with the single exception of the

systematic manner in which their party was strengthened during

our route from the schooner to the village.
